subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN INTEREST RATES ON INSURED LOANS

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Public Works):
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF INCREASE IN INTEREST RATES ON INSURED LOANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform hon. members of the decision to increase the maximum interest rate on insured loans under part I of the National Housing Act from 51 per cent to 5J per cent. Corresponding increases will take place with respect to rates applicable to the other types of loans under the act. These rates are ceiling rates. Lenders are, of course, free to make loans at lesser rates if circumstances so warrant.
The statute authorizes the governor in council to fix the maximum rate of interest that may be charged for various types of loans. In respect of insured mortgage loans, the interest rate cannot exceed the yield on long-term government securities, plus 21 per cent as of the time the rate is fixed.
It is the expressed policy of the government to adjust the mortgage interest rate from time to time within the provisions of the statutory formula so that the lowest rate will be established which will attract on the market adequate mortgage funds. In accordance with this policy the rate was reduced from 5J per cent to 51 per cent in February, 1955. It is now felt that rates under the act should revert to their former levels.
Actually, the interest rate on long-term government bonds would have justified an 67509-124
increase from 51 per cent to 5J per cent last August, but the flow of funds to housing then, and until quite recently, has been good, with the result that no such action has been taken. Bearing in mind the continued high level of interest rates in general and the anticipated demand on investible funds in 1956, an increase is necessary now so that builders and home owners will have continued access to mortgage funds under the National Housing Act in the year ahead.
The change in the interest rate will have effect Monday morning, the 12th of March.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Is he in a position to give any report regarding the apparently critical situation in the Middle East, and when he is replying will he tell the house and the country why the government adopt different principles in regard to arms sold by a contractor to the Egyptian air force than in sales by a government corporation dealing with Israel?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON SITUATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, though I did not receive notice of this question I rather anticipated that it might be asked, or one like it, and I therefore welcome the opportunity of making a statement on the matter referred to by my hon. friend, namely the situation in the Middle East.
The situation in that area, particularly the relations between Israel and her Arab neighbours, has been tense and the cause of potential conflict since the first day of Israel's existence.
There have been ups and downs in the position, but it has always been disturbing and worrying. Events of last week have added to our worries. However, there have been in the last year more immediately disturbing developments, such as the El Auja and lake Tiberias incidents, which did not result in conflict, and we must hope that not

only will conflict be avoided now but, more
important, that the cause of conflict will be
removed.
The situation, Mr. Speaker, seems to have eased somewhat in the last few days following the shock caused by the abrupt dismissal of Sir John Glubb from the Arab legion of Jordan and there have been somewhat reassuring statements from Middle East leaders.
Hon. members will have noted that Premier Ben-Gurion said on Wednesday: "This government will not start a war". At the same time, it was stated in Washington, from what are referred to as official sources, that there was nothing to indicate that an attack from either side was imminent.
The governments of the United States, the United Kingdom and France have been in consultation with a view to doing everything possible to avoid armed conflict in the area, and we ourselves are keeping in close touch with -these governments on this and other matters almost -daily.
Hon. members will also have noted that the Secretary General of the United Nations, a careful man not given to exaggeration or overoptimism, has recently stated his considered view, in reply to a question as to whether the Middle East was on the brink of war, that "We have moved away from the brink". He did not believe that there would be war, and he added that it was "even a little premature in his opinion to say that an arms race had developed".
It is true that during the week there have been disturbing reports of border incidents, but it should also be noted -that neither Israel nor her neighbours have -considered these serious enough, or as representing a dangerous enough development to warrant a request that the United Nations security council be called to deal with an imminent threat to peace; something that they have not hesitated to do in the past.
My view, therefore, is that the situation, while tense and difficult, as it has been for years, and while giving no ground for -complacency and much for anxiety, is not such as to warrant interference in the shipment by a Canadian company of a few training planes which were equipped with no -arms whatever and could not be made structurally effective for that purpose without at least two months' factory work. Such a shipment should not add to tensions or dangers in the area and could not upset any balance of armed strength between -contending parties, nor does it represent in any way favouring one of those parties against the other. The record of the government in this matter over the years sufficiently disposes of that idea.
Inquiries of the Ministry
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like to repeat, and to emphasize what has already been said in this house, that neither Israel nor any of the Arab governments concerned can hope to gain anything from a resort to arms to settle their present differences. On the contrary, war would be disastrous to all concerned. It would result in the mobilization of world opinion, in the United Nations and elsewhere, in condemnation of the aggressor and in support for the victim of aggression. I cannot believe that this is a situation which any country in the Middle East desires to bring about. I can give this house and the country an assurance that the Canadian government will play its part with other friendly governments in efforts, especially through the United Nations, to avoid -any such disaster and in helping to bring about peace and stability in that area.

Mr. Chairman, last week when the adjournment of this debate took place I was speaking about fishery problems. May I now join with the other hon. members of this house in welcoming the minister back to his seat. I do so because this department needs a head and when the head is away it does not get the consideration it should.
Many questions have been raised during this debate regarding territorial waters and our jurisdiction over them. May I say that in the debate in the committee on fisheries in 1953 we examined a bill entitled "an act to protect the coastal fisheries". That was on February 13, 1953. An extended examination of that bill took place. For the benefit of those hon. members who do not appear to understand what the three-mile limit
means I wish to quote from the proceedings of the fisheries committee dated February 9, 1953. At that time the minister was replying to some questions on this matter and he said this:
It was this matter of territorial waters to which most of the debate related. We have had such debates on previous occasions when fisheries bills were up. The desire of most fishermen in Canada is understandable, that our territorial waters be extended out as far as possible to preserve the inshore fisheries.
In reply to a question which I asked him the minister made this reply:
The French and the Americans still have certain rights on the Newfoundland coasts; but fishing on the Grand Banks is probably a very good example of the fact that in the background the British, in respect to having freedom of the seas, as do many nations, feel that they have a historic right in the fisheries which are not within our three mile limit, but which may be upon our continental shelf.
On that occasion I quoted the judgment of the international court at The Hague. Without going into too much detail, I should like to put on record some of that judgment. This is what I said at that time, as recorded on page 11 of the minutes of proceedings of the committee:
The 20th day of October, 1818-Convention signed at London between Great Britain and the United States on the 20th day of October, 1818. That was the first. That dispute was taken before The Hague court, and now I will read the judgment. The judgment of the court at The Hague was as follows:
In case of bays the three marine miles are to be measured from a straight line drawn across the body of water at the place where it ceases to have the configuration and characteristics of a bay. At all other places the three marine miles are to be measured following the sinuosities of the coast.
Here is the judgment:
Now therefore this Tribunal in pursuance of the provisions of Art. IV hereby recommends for the consideration and acceptance of the high contracting parties the following rules and method of procedure for determining the limits of the bays hereinbefore enumerated.
1.	In every bay not hereinafter specifically provided for the limits of exclusion shall be drawn three miles seaward from a straight line across the bay in the part nearest the entrance at the first point where the width does not exceed ten miles.
2.	In the following bays where the configuration of the coast and the local climatic conditions are such that foreign fishermen when within the geographic headlands might reasonably and bona fide believe themselves on the high seas, the limits of exclusion shall be drawn in each case between the headlands hereinafter specified as being those at and within which such fishermen might be reasonably expected to recognize the bay under average conditions.
Then it goes on to specify certain bays. It specifies Fortune bay, in Newfoundland and, as may be of great interest to my friend,

the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, is specifies the bay of Fundy. It goes on to say:
It is understood that nothing in these rules refers either to the bay of Fundy considered as a whole part from its bays and creeks or as to the innocent passage through the Gut of Canso, which were excluded by the agreement made by exchange of notes between Mr. Bacon and Mr. Bryce dated February 21, 1909, and March 4, 1909; or to Conception bay, which was provided for by the decision of the Privy Council in the case of the Direct United States Cable Company v. The Anglo American Telegraph Company, in which decision the United States have acquiesced.
Now we come to the crux of the whole matter of the three-mile jurisdiction. After the international tribunal at The Hague made the ruling on the three-mile limit, that was not found satisfactory over a period of years. The matter was debated by the league of nations, but no decision was arrived at there. It was taken from the league of nations to the United Nations, with the same result, so that today the three-mile limit is recognized by certain countries and not recognized by others. It may be interesting to note which countries favour three miles and which countries favour 12 miles. I was quoting from Sessional Papers, Volume XLV, No. 24, 1911. I also quoted from the Digest of International Law by Hackworth, Volume I, chapters I-V, page 628:
Various points of view with reference to the breadth of the territorial waters were expressed provisionally or in principle in the second committee of the Conference for the Codification of International Law held at The Hague in 1930, at its thirteenth meeting held on April 3. The delegates of certain states were in favour of the acceptance of the principle of a zone on the high sea contiguous to the territorial sea in which the coastal state would be able to exercise certain control. The views as expressed in the meeting of April 3 on these subjects were summarized as follows: Union of South Africa, 3 miles; Germany, 3 miles; United States, 3 miles; Belgium, 3 miles; Great Britain, 3 miles; Canada, 3 miles; Chile, 6 or 3 miles; China, 3 miles; Colombia, 6 miles; Cuba, 6 miles; Denmark, 3 miles, Spain, 6 miles; Finland, 4 miles-
-and perhaps what is more important to us in Newfoundland-
-Italy, 6 miles; Poland, 3 miles; and Portugal, 12 or 6 miles.
So you will see generally from this that the matter has not been finally settled yet.
It was interesting for us to note that Portugal favoured a 12-mile limit, because Portuguese trawlers go out year after year fishing on the Grand Banks off Newfoundland and also fishing in our territorial waters outside the three-mile limit. We in Newfoundland believe that the Grand Banks are the breeding place of the codfish that come to our shores in such numbers year by year and we believe that, as a result of this intensive fishing that is going on at the Grand Banks at the present time, there are signs

I have spoken on this before and I cannot emphasize too strongly today, as far as the future fisheries of the codfish in Newfoundland are concerned, particularly on the southwest coast and certain parts of the northeast coast, that this matter will have to be pursued with the governments of Spain, France and Portugal so that some international agreement may be reached and some form of conservation may be agreed to between the countries. I make this plea this morning because I think that in the course of time we shall have to do something about it.
With regard to the territorial waters, again it may be interesting to note that quite lately Peru and Ecuador extended their jurisdiction over the territorial waters up to 200 miles. They seized fishing boats well off the coast, about 200 miles out, and brought them in to port. They were released only after a fine had been paid. It may be interesting to note also a statement by President Truman in 1945 regarding the continental shelf. I quote from page 16 of the report of the proceedings of the committee on February 9, 1953:
In 1945 President Truman made two declarations on a statement of policy of the United States government. One of those declarations related to the continental shelf in which the United States claimed sovereignty over the subsoil resources in the continental shelf and at the same time made it very clear that the character of the waters above it remained unaffected.
This means that the United States claims jurisdiction over the continental shelf but not the waters above it. It may be interesting to note also that the United States has certain fishing rights on the south coast of Newfoundland. The Grand Banks are part of the continental shelf off the coast of Newfoundland. Now that the United States has claimed jurisdictional sovereignty over the continental shelf, it may be that in the course of time there will be one step further, that they claim jurisdiction over the waters above the continental shelf. If this takes place, Canada will be in a position to claim jurisdiction over the Grand Banks.
The time has come, in all this confusion in international law about the three-mile limit and whether it should be three miles, ten miles or 12 miles, for a decision to be arrived at by someone. Somebody has to take the lead in this matter. I advocate now without

Supply-Fisheries
any reservation that Canada, which in international affairs is playing its part so brilliantly, now take the lead and notify the other powers that it will extend jurisdiction over its continental shelf for the full 12 miles. That is quite a statement for me to make, but I am convinced that somebody must give the lead and I believe that Canada is the proper one to do it. This government must take its courage in both hands, make that announcement and stick by it. I believe that if we do that other nations will follow our example and, instead of having a three-mile territorial jurisdiction, which is in dispute so often, we would settle the matter once and for all, and most of the countries in the world would accept the 12-mile limit. That is all I have to say regarding the territorial jurisdiction over our waters.
There is one point in this discussion on fisheries that I think is very important. I have studied the set-up of the fisheries organization of the federal department in British Columbia. Let me say right here that as a result of my visit, there a few years ago I was amazed at the efficiency of the officials, their grasp of the situation there and their control over the fisheries of British Columbia. I discussed this matter with Mr. Mayhew, who was then Minister of Fisheries, and said, "We want that kind of organization on the east coast of Canada." Our fisheries are being organized, it is true, and many improvements have been made in the last three or four years, but until we have such an organization on the east coast as they are on the west coast of Canada our fisheries are going to suffer. Let me give you my views of an outline of fishery prospects for the whole of North America. On the Pacific coast all or practically all fisheries are regulated. They are regulated because if intensive fishing takes place depletion will also take place and to preserve the fisheries on the west coast of Canada conservation measures must be taken and have been taken in conjunction with the United States of America. Therefore if you cannot catch any more fish-I use the term "fish" in its broadest sense

on the west coast without depletion you can understand that you cannot increase your catch there very much. The same situation has taken place on the fishing banks off the New England coast. The same thing is true off the Nova Scotia coast.
Therefore the only natural fishing resource left in the whole of North America today is Newfoundland, Labrador and possibly Greenland. You have 170 million people in the United States and Canada with a natural increase of about 4 million a year. These people have to be housed, clothed and fed.

If the fishing industry is to supply the increasing population and the big demand of these 170 million odd people for fishery products, they will have to go further afield and look for the natural product. The only place left for them to go is Newfoundland and Labrador.
Evidence of that has been plainly shown during the last two or three years when we have had Nova Scotia merchants coming from Nova Scotia to Newfoundland to buy our salted codfish in its raw state. That tendency is going to increase. Therefore it is necessary in my opinion that a complete survey of the fishery prospects of the whole of the east coast of Canada be undertaken without delay. It will be too late when depletion takes place. The time to begin that is now. In that connection I should like to point to the Atlantic salmon. Many years ago we used to catch Atlantic salmon in very large quantities, but the catch has been decreasing year by year and the need for preservation of the salmon and for conservation methods has reached such a state now that something drastic will have to be done.
Last year I also mentioned our herring fishery. The herring used to come into Fortune bay literally in millions. For some reason or other they left Fortune bay and about a year or so later they struck into bay of Islands. In the last two or three years they have been leaving bay of Islands. Nobody knows where the herring go or the reason for this coming and going. In answer to a question of mine last year, the minister said that the lack of fishery scientists was the cause of the delay in making a survey of the herring fishery. I do hope that in the coming year something definite will be done so that we may know more about our herring, where they go and why they do not come into our shores regularly. Our herring fishery has become a very important fishery. The demand for our herring is increasing and prices are good. When the minister is replying perhaps he might say something about this matter.
I was very glad to hear the minister say the other day that the salt codfish industry is beginning to look up. It is only two or three years ago that we had a depression in the industry. I am glad to see that the methods adopted by the Department of Trade and Commerce in the marketing of our salt codfish are beginning to have beneficial results, and I must give credit where credit is due. I am very glad to hear that we have no surplus of salt codfish this year. In fact, prices are beginning to become better. This is a matter of great satisfaction to our fishermen because they have been fishing under very adverse conditions for a number of years. This will

encourage our fishermen to continue their calling and go out on the high seas to earn their daily bread.
The parliamentary assistant to the Postmaster General, who comes from a fishing community in Nova Scotia, made a statement the other day with which I wholly agree. He appealed for wharves and breakwaters to protect our fishermen in the different places from which they fish. I agree wholeheartedly with what he said, and I should like to give one example now of what happened in my riding in a place like Whiteway where they never had any protection or wharves. They asked me whether I could get them a wharf. So badly were they in need of a wharf for protection that they offered to work on it if the timber could be supplied. The wharf was built. It is a wharf and breakwater combined. The very day that the wharf was completed 5,000 pounds of mackerel were landed on the wharf. That was early in September and from September until November, when the mackerel fishing season ended, 250,000 pounds of mackerel were landed on the wharf. That is encouraging, and we want more encouragement.
We like to see our friends from Nova Scotia come and buy our fish. We place no restrictions on them. It creates competition with our own merchants and the consequence is that our fishermen probably get a better price. But how long the people from Nova Scotia will come there to buy our raw material is a matter of doubt because what has been happening is that they come there, buy our raw fish, process it and sell it in the markets in which we sell it. The time is coming when we are going to process our own fish.
This makes it all the more important that there should, as I said a moment ago, be conservation. The fisheries must be regulated on the east coast as they are on the west coast. Some control must be exercised, some organization must be set up similar to that on the west coast, and I think the time to do it is now. There is not much more I can say regarding the fisheries on the east coast except that reference has been made to the number of fishermen decreasing. When the minister replies I should like him to give me statistics for the last five years as to the number of fishermen so that we may know definitely one way or the other whether our fishermen are leaving the industry or whether they are staying with it. Some people think our fishermen are leaving the industry, and in some places they may be. If this is a fact, then it is all the more reason for regulations and for encouragement to our fishermen to carry on their vocation in life 67509-125

so that this industry, which is becoming more important to Canada day by day may, be preserved.
I am not going to talk any more about the nutritious food which comes from the sea, but it is increasingly evident to me in Ottawa and other places I visit that the people of Canada are becoming more fish conscious than ever. If we are to supply the demand we must preserve the natural elements of our fishery products so that Canada may get the food which is required and so that our fishermen may get the returns which are so justly due them.

I would be very ungrateful, Mr. Chairman, if I did not first say how much I appreciate the courtesy of the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) last Friday when he said he would hold over an item in the estimates dealing with lamprey control until I was present. I am very glad, too, that he indicated 'to the house I was speaking to a group on Friday night and dealt to a great extent with the efforts of this government, in partnership with the United States government, in connection with conservation. I should like to tell the minister, too, that the group was much larger than I expected, numbering some 450 as a matter of fact, who were conservation conscious. I was amazed that in that little area in southwestern Ontario people should gather in such large numbers because they were concerned about fish and wildlife and other aspects of conservation.
In the course of the discussion afterwards, and even prior to the meeting, it became quite apparent why they were so vitally concerned. I think I should make a point of this when I deal with the lamprey situation, and I should like to deal with that now rather than wait until that particular item is called in case I am not here then. All you need to do is to look at any good map of Ontario to note the number of streams that flow into Georgian bay, lake Huron and lake Superior which are infested with this curse of the fishing industry, the lamprey, to note how seriously it will affect fishing in these areas. The point I should like to emphasize just now is that this will seriously affect the tourist revenue of the Dominion of Canada. Three or four years ago I wondered why some people were not going back to areas in northern Ontario in which there was good fishing, that is speckled trout and other types of trout. I have learned since that it was because the lamprey had gotten into the streams and into the lakes and, as a matter of fact, had made sport fishing a bygone sport in those particular areas. I think that is a viewpoint we must not overlook because after all is said and
What size are they?

Oh, about four, five or six pounds. If that happens, the lamprey will destroy the commercial fishing industry in the great lakes. The point I should like to emphasize is, as I said a moment ago, that this job that faces the international joint commission is much bigger than we expected. Here is a department of fisheries report and I think I should put on the record what it says at page 52. It shows to what extent efforts have been made to eliminate this curse of the fishing industry, and what vital efforts must be made now and later to rehabilitate the industry in those areas. Now, this deals with lake Superior:
The lamprey control program which is presently confined to lake Superior, the last stronghold of the valuable lake trout in the Great Lakes system, was forwarded by federal funds and the co-operation of provincial personnel of the Department of Lands and Forests. Approximately 600 streams tributary to lake Superior on the Canadian side of the lake were surveyed and assessed as potential lamprey spawning streams.
Mr. Chairman, it is going to be a terrific challenge to man to combat this predator because if there are that many spawning streams on the Canadian side there may be that many on the United States side or even more. Last session it was suggested that effort would be confined to lake Superior to hold the line. I disagreed with that idea and l still do. I quarrel with the suggestion of the provincial department of government on this idea of having hatcheries and restocking the lakes. I think we all agree that if it becomes necessary to assist nature to rehabilitate the fishing industry, it can be done only through hatcheries. Some argument developed last fall between myself and the fishermen on one side and an official of the Ontario government on the other side who contended that

restocking the lakes and keeping the hatcheries open was like spitting in the ocean. At that time I said and I think it is worth while repeating-that they had had a grand experience in that activity because that is all they have been doing over the last several years, namely spitting in the ocean.
Just recently, as a matter of fact, a statement came out from much higher authority in that particular government saying how successful they were in stocking some inland lakes with trout and so on. But the stocking of lakes or the restocking of them is a sort of relative term. You can stock a small lake with maybe a few thousand trout and it would be a successful operation. But a few thousand trout in lake Huron or in lake Superior would be like spitting in the ocean, and it would be a small spit if we bad that many dumped in the Atlantic or the Pacific ocean. It is therefore a relative term. If we are going to accomplish anything in these commercial fishing areas, the figure must be in the millions or billions of finger-lings.
I am going to emphasize here my own opinion which is substantiated by the fishermen in my area and, I am sure, by other fishermen. In the first place, let us make a joint attack. Let us make the attack in lake Huron as well as in lake Superior. The other day the minister indicated that United States scientists had perfected a jelly or some poisonous substance which could exterminate four or five generations of lamprey while they are still in the mud. That was certainly good news because, as we know, these lampreys stay in the mud for four years before they ever go out to the great lakes. When they go out they are four or five inches long and when they come back to spawn they are 20 to 24 inches long. That is the growth in one year, and indicates the amount of food they have consumed and the damage which they can do. I therefore submit that we must gamble a little bit.
In the first place we must get more money for this project to eliminate this curse to the fishing industry not only in lake Superior but in the other inland lakes. We must get more money to enable the joint commission to make that joint attack. If we wait, with respect to lake Huron, until the lamprey is exterminated in lake Superior, that will be at the earliest-if all the lampreys can be exterminated-a matter of four or five years. I think that is recognized as being a fair estimate. It might be 8 or 10 years before they are exterminated. In the meantime the lamprey will have become so injurious to the industry in lake Huron and in the other lakes below that there will not be any fishing 67509-125J

I am going to say in conclusion, Mr. Chairman, that the people to whom I have spoken, who are in the commercial fishing industry, are more satisfied today than ever before that the necessary steps will be taken by this joint commission, through their respective governments, to rehabilitate the fishing industry. Uike the fishermen of all those great lakes, I regret that the setting up of this commission was not proceeded with years ago. It is unfortunate for this country and unfortunate for those who border the United States, and for the people of both countries, that the eight states bordering on the great lakes and our own province were so dilatory. They knew the challenge before them and yet they made picayune attempts not only to curb or destroy the lamprey but to rehabilitate an industry which they knew was dying because of the lack of co-operative efforts to exterminate this curse of the industry.
As one of the members of the committee-I was not a member at first but I was put on purposely with this particular project in mind, and I hope that if another committee is set up I shall be given the same honour, and there are others whose constituencies border on the great lakes who are equally interested-may I say I feel satisfied in my own mind that

because of the many representations made to the minister, which he can forward to his associates in the government, more money will be made available for this purpose. It is going to take more money. I think the minister himself will say that. To be frank about it, we cannot fight this menace with $1 million a year from both governments, nor can we even curb it, let alone exterminate it. I have no doubt in my mind that when one considers the number of streams that flow into lake Superior alone, apart from those that flow into other lakes-we know now that they spawn in lake Erie-it may take $3 million, $4 million or $5 million a year before this menace is exterminated. Mr. Chairman, I should like at this time to make a few observations in relation to the fishery industry as applied more particularly to my own part of the country. Before I do so I also wish to express my delight at the clear indications of the minister's improving health. It was gratifying indeed, during the course of his address last Friday, to be able to observe that he is now on the road to full recovery of his former good health and aggressiveness.
During his remarks the minister made some reference to the Canadian Fisherman's Loan Act which was passed by parliament during last year's session. I am personally interested in this measure because I expect many beneficial results from its operation. However, I remain somewhat apprehensive that one probable drawback in this connection will be the over-caution with which the banks will avail themselves of this legislation. But, as happened with the Farm Improvement Loans Act, it is hoped that, in due course of time, the banks will again realize the advantages of these government-guaranteed loans. Indeed, it is important that this legislation be

made wholly operative if it is to provide all the assistance which it is intended to provide to our fishermen.
Following the introduction of this legislation in the house last year, we recall that an amendment was introduced enabling credit unions to participate in this loan project. This amendment followed representations made by the credit union associations before the fisheries committee. The opportunities requested in these representations were granted, and I trust our credit unions will now avail themselves of these new opportunities of serving their members who wish to take advantage of this policy. We must acknowledge that a great number of credit union members live in rural areas, where they have not been accustomed to deal with banks. We know, of course, that in many instances lack of capital may prevent the individual credit union from engaging freely in these transactions. We would expect, however, that through their federations suitable arrangements could be made to obtain the necessary capital to meet this purpose.
On different occasions in this house, Mr. Chairman, I have spoken of the urgent need of restoring the oyster industry along the southeastern New Brunswick shores. In the Buctouche-Cocagne-Grande Digue area alone at one time this industry represented an annual net income of over $30,000. It was similar in importance to the Richibucto area.
I wish to repeat now what I have already stated on other occasions in this house, that within the past few years our oyster beds have become completely unproductive. I know that the officials of the department are aware of these conditions and are endeavouring in every way to restore the productivity of these oyster beds. It was my privilege last summer to accompany two of these officials on a survey to secure new data on the situation. I only hope that these endeavours will be maintained. The restoration of the oyster industry along our shores is of great significance to the general economy of our fishing population.
I believe I should now stress before this committee the importance of having an educational program for our fishermen. I again recall with satisfaction the experiment undertaken two years ago among our lobster fishermen. This, I can assure you, has been greatly beneficial. It is remarkable that many of those fishermen who took exception to the scientific principles expounded at that time are now endorsing those self-same principles.

I must bring to the attention of this committee the necessity of providing our fishing centres with more freezing and storage facilities for fresh fish. A few of these plants are now operating along the shores and the results provide positive evidence of how-profitable it would be to possess more of these plants. I am pleased to note that a co-operative enterprise at Richibucto has recently laid plans to engage in this modern process of fish conservation. I refer to the Cartier Co-op. which last year purchased a large, all-equipped plant, ready for operation. The project involves a number of fishermen from the northern part of Kent county. The activities of the Department of Fisheries, Mr. Chairman, are of great interest to the people of the maritimes. Many depend upon fishing for their livelihood. It is true that the standard of living of our fishing communities has been greatly improved during the last few years, but a still greater measure of economic stability is essential. I urge upon the government, through its Department of Fisheries, that it use every means and put forth every effort to promote this aim.

I too, Mr. Chairman, am very pleased to see the minister in his seat and again performing his functions as Minister of Fisheries. I think I can safely say that, so far as the people of British Columbia are concerned, as long as we must have a Liberal government we would rather have the minister who is now occupying this post occupy it. I believe he has proved himself as able a cabinet minister as the people of British Columbia have ever had in Ottawa. His responsibilities are tremendous indeed. When he took over the Department of Fisheries the department was in for a rough ride from one end of Canada to the other. Fortunately we seem to have overcome most of the major problems for the time being that faced the fishermen in British Columbia.
However, as was pointed out a short time ago the fishermen on the great lakes still have that great problem of the lamprey and there

is the problem of the rehabilitation of the whole fishing industry in the maritimes and in what I understand is supposed to be called the Atlantic province of Newfoundland. I am pleased to see that some progress is being made towards this rehabilitation of the eastern fisheries. However, I should like to call the minister's attention to a few other matters. I know that the Minister of Public Works is responsible for all major construction efforts of the federal government. However, I believe the Minister of Public Works, from the statements he has made, relies to a very great extent on his colleagues in the cabinet for informing him of the needs of their particular departments. I am hoping that the Minister of Fisheries will soon speak to the Minister of Public Works and outline to him the need for a fairly large number of rather inexpensive wharves suitable for the fishermen in the lower mainland areas.
I know that a great new fishermen's wharf is being built at the city of Vancouver. However, I have been given to understand that that wharf is already overcrowded before it is completed. Many of these fishermen live in the rural areas around the city of Vancouver and if small wharf facilities could be supplied to them, say, along the shores of Burrard Inlet or the Fraser river or Pitt river, I am sure these facilities would be very much appreciated.
I should like to call the minister's attention to another fact, though he may be already fully aware of it. I feel that some more public relations work might be done to develop closer understanding among the fishermen on the west coast of the intentions of his department. The fishermen of the Fraser river are not yet convinced of the need for the closing of the fishing above Westminster bridge. Some of them have lived there 40 or 50 years, have their homes there and are well established far away from the deep sea fishing. The minister's efforts thus far to convince them of the need in the interests of conservation to limit their ability to fish in the districts where they are used to fishing have thus far not been too successful and have not been as successful as they should be. Either his argument is very weak or not enough effort has been put forth in explanations to the men.
I should also like to reiterate the demand that others have made, I believe, in this house from time to time, that some move be made to establish our territorial waters in British Columbia from land's end in the north to land's end in the south, if I might put it that way. The people in my constituency feel that those waters that would be enclosed by such a line ought to be rightfully claimed as our own waters.

I was very pleased to read the minister's statement on page 1748 of Hansard, in connection with power development, in which he said:
We feel, first of all, that every non-salmon stream in the province should be developed for power before a salmon stream is touched. In that respect, we feel that, before the Fraser is touched, that part of the Columbia river in Canada should be exploited to the full.
I hope the minister is very keenly aware of the fact that unless the federal government, which last year assumed some responsibility for power development on the Columbia river, undertakes some initiative in the matter of early development of power in the Columbia basin, the federal government may find the provincial government making a deal that will completely frustrate the good intentions of the minister. Because of the failure of initiative on the part of the federal government, we may see the British Columbia government take some action that most Canadians might have reason to regret.
I am pleased to hear the minister report that some progress is being made in the means that have been initiated by his department to aid fishermen and that loans are now available. I hope the use of these loans will be more actively advocated by the minister's department. I believe the insurance feature is coming into widespread use, and I know that the department has given serious consideration to making all fishermen eligible for unemployment insurance. There is a demand, as the minister well knows, all over Canada for the inclusion of fishermen under the Unemployment Insurance Act, and I hope that a year from now some satisfactory means will have been found.
The section of the house to which I belong, the C.C.F., will always support any Minister of Fisheries in any conservation measures that he will undertake. Within the limits of adequate conservation measures, we do, however, adhere to the philosophy of full production for the people of our nation, and going along with that, and equally necessary, is a policy of complete and full distribution of what we are able to produce. This applies to the fishing industry as well.
We are pleased to see the minister playing a very active role in his department in the field of international co-operation as regards the fishing industry. I should like at this time to express my appreciation of the fact that, as I have noted in the report on the Fisheries Prices Support Act, the department came to the aid of the cod fishermen and also to the aid of hungry people in the world in that they supplied over $900,000 worth of codfish to the hungry peoples of Greece and
Supply-Fisheries
of South Korea. Only this morning I again had a look at the mail, which I receive so very often from people in my riding asking me to do what I can to see to it that Canada's surplus foodstuffs are used to feed the hungry people of the world. This action on the part of the prices support board, which is under the minister's jurisdiction, was a most notable one and will receive the hearty endorsation of the Canadian public at large. I note that the fisheries prices support board paid half of the cost of this large gift and the Department of External Affairs paid for approximately the other half. We could well have many more such programs.
However, the cause of Canadians using their surplus foodstuffs in the interest of aiding world peace, I feel, has been harmed somewhat by the deal that the fisheries prices support board made in the case of herring bloaters, and I should like to spend a few minutes on that. The report states that herring bloaters were purchased through the prices support board to protect the 1954 herring industry. Those who held unsold stocks of herring bloaters were advised to submit their offers by June 30, 1954. I notice as a result of the offers received the board purchased, under the authority of an order in council passed on June 30, 1954, a total of 72,929 boxes for which they paid 80 cents or 55 cents a box, depending on grade. These prices were paid, in the words of the report, "at producer's plant or in storage." According to the report, these herring bloaters were not sold at prevailing market prices because one of the reasons for the purchase was to preserve the stability of the market and therefore it was considered inadvisable to sell them at a reduced price. Eventually the bloaters were sold to a reduction plant to be used for the manufacture of fertilizer, and these 18 pound boxes of herring bloaters were sold at 9 cents a box.
It is to be noted that the freight charges on the herring to the reduction plant exceeded $9,000 and the net returns to the prices support board from the sale were slightly in excess of $6,000. One is rather inclined to ask why the government would pay $9,129.56 to haul a lot of herring to a reduction plant and sell them there for the sum of $6,563.61. It seems that not only were the fish given to the reduction plant for nothing but the government added some $3,000 in order to deliver the fish at the doors of the reduction plant.
When I received the report I put a question on the order paper. Question No. 73, as found at page 1190 of Hansard, reads:
Before the passing of order in council P.C. 1934-931, June 30, 1954, authorizing the sale of
I do not like to interrupt but I am so surprised that they should be called choice. Would you tell me again where they are described as choice?

If the minister will look at page 8 of the report he will see that in the first paragraph it says:
In all, 72,929 boxes were purchased by the board. Of these, only 257 were choice grade of the 1952 pack.
That is all it says, and it also says that with respect to 1953 production purchases were to be of standard grade.
That is right.

I think the minister will have to agree that his reply was not very accurately worded. Possibly that is more or less a minor matter. However, the minister goes on to say in his answer:
The Department of Trade and Commerce did make inquires in the Belgian Congo where the product is known, but no interest could be developed.
I was a little surprised when I saw that because I have never heard of the people in the Belgian Congo being very hungry and I had asked whether any attempt had been made to supply these choice and standard quality fish to some of the hungry people of the world. Therefore I asked a further question. I asked at what time and in what manner were these inquiries made

and were any replies received. I got a reply from the Department of Trade and Commerce saying that on December 1, 1953, an airmail letter was dispatched to Leopoldville and a reply was sent from there on December 14, 1953, saying that no interest could be developed in the Belgian Congo.
My quarrel with the answer is that the date supplied me here as to the time of the inquiry indicates that this was merely a routine piece of information supplied by the Department of Trade and Commerce to the trade commissioners, certainly the trade commissioner in Leopoldville, as to the possibilities of finding a market where we could sell our herring. That was completely evading the question I had asked, namely, whether any attempt had been made to find any place where we could dispose of these admittedly good fish as a gift.
A few moments ago I endorsed the actions of the fisheries prices support board. When we have surplus fish, by all means let all taxpayers share the cost of helping the industry, protecting the price and using the fish as a method of expressing our good will to needy people in whatever part of the world they may live. However, I feel that in this case somebody blundered somewhere because these herring were bought with the taxpayers' money at 80 cents and 55 cents per box and at a subsidized rate were sold for reduction purposes at 9 cents a box. I do not think such action helps the cause of the fisheries prices support board or the intentions of the minister with respect thereto. It may be that the minister does not have enough funds available to supervise adequately what may be relatively minor operations in his department. In looking at the amount of money in the estimates for the various ministers for the coming year I notice that, next to the Secretary of State, the Minister of Fisheries receives the least of all.
Very economical.

I notice that he is even getting less money this year than he got last year. I do not know why he is asking for less money. Possibly the Minister of Finance may have been particularly harsh with the minister when he spoke to him. I think an amount of $12,753,283 out of a federal budget of $5 billion is hardly adequate for the fisheries industry in relation to the value of that industry and the great need on the Atlantic seaboard. I fully sympathize with the minister and I only hope that the cause of using surplus food supplies to help needy people in the world and thereby also help-

more because of deals such as the one involved here in the giving away of these herring.

This development, Mr. Chairman, is due to the fact that recently new industries have been set up in my constituency, whereas an older well established firm, the Gorton Pew Company, which operates salt fish plants on the islands, has turned one of these into a frozen fillet plant. Moreover, I am told that this company, which operated its plants at Grindstone, plans to build a new one at Amherst. There is also in my constituency a company by the name of Canapro, which produces fish meal.
I am glad of this improvement and diversification of our production but, at the same time, I wish to point out that the change should not be too radical. We should not produce frozen fillets and fish meal only. We should continue also to produce smoked herring and salt cod, as we did in the past, because we must keep our traditional outlets for these products and, as the old proverb says, we should not put all our eggs in the same basket.
If we carry out too radical a change and if our market for frozen cod fillets and fish meal should slump, we might find ourselves in a very bad situation if we did not carry on with our salted and smoked products industry as we have done up till now.
The figures I have just quoted to the committee, Mr. Chairman, amply show that progress is being made in the Magdalen islands. I am glad to point them out and to express my appreciation to the government, as well as to private enterprise, for all they have done towards increasing the yield of the island fisheries. However, there is still much to be done in this field and, merely to give the committee an idea of how much remains to be done, I shall quote a paragraph from a letter which has come to me from one of my constituents:
To give you an idea of the average income of the islands cod fishermen, here is the case of two associated fishermen of my acquaintance, whose catch for the last fishing season amounted to 40,000 pounds of fresh cod and 12,000 pounds of salt cod, sold for a gross income of $1,800.
If you deduct from that amount the costs of equipment, upkeep of the boat, fuel, salt, etc., the individual net income is less than $600. The situation is such that a great many young men who

like fishing have to go outside the islands to find a trade far less interesting but far more profitable.
That is why, Mr. Chairman, I submit that we must continue to help our fishermen-

Mr. Chairman, at one o'clock I was saying that the income of the Magdalen islands fishermen was very low and that we should continue to try and help them increase it. I would have a few suggestions to make to the department in that connection.
During the last session of this parliament we passed an act to help fishermen to get loans in order to buy equipment. That act is now in force. However I have received complaints from my electors who claim that it is not much help to them on the ground that in order to be able to borrow from the banks on part of their equipment they have to pay in cash at least 30 per cent of the purchase price for new equipment and 40 per cent for used equipment. They tell me, on the islands, that these terms are not favourable enough and that they do not really help fishermen.
Those who have the means to pay such large cash amounts can deal directly with the merchants who are ready to sell them their goods for 30 or 40 per cent down. If we really want to have a law which will help the fishermen to buy the equipment they lack, through loans from the bank, the minimum down payment should be reduced.
The hon. minister said in his speech that the number of applications for these loans was comparatively small. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this shows the value of my argument and that the rather small number of applications is due to the facts I just mentioned to the committee.

Now, the federal government allows the fishermen a grant of $165 a ton when they build new fishing vessels. We even find in the estimates an amount of $200,000 to that effect. Unfortunately, the act is not administered by the federal government, but by the governments of the various provinces, and there is not enough co-operation between the federal and provincial governments in the selection of those who are entitled to these grants. The decision is up to the provincial government. Well, without going into details, it can easily be understood that the choice the provincial government of Quebec makes with regard to the people entitled to the grants is not always the one I would make myself. I therefore suggest that the federal government control the allocation of these grants and decide as to whom they should be made.
As a matter of fact, this situation brings about some extraordinary anomalies. For instance, if a fisherman wants to get a grant of $165 for his fishing vessel, he has to go through the provincial loan office and borrow from the provincial government, even if he has enough money to pay the difference. In other words, our fishermen of the Magdalen islands cannot get the federal government grant of $165 a ton without having to borrow from the provincial government, even if they don't need to do so. Then, what happens when a fisherman has all the money he needs, except for the $165 a ton grant, is that he borrows $1 from the provincial government in order to qualify for the grant.
Mr. Chairman, I submit that we have here an anomaly of which we should rid ourselves. I understand that, when this grants policy was agreed upon, the Department of Fisheries didn't have as many employees, and its administrative services were not as well organized as they are now, but I feel that with its increasing importance, the greater number of its employees, its improved administrative services, it is time this department look after the distribution of these grants.
Mr. Chairman, I wish also to deal with the matter of lobster trap insurance. This insurance brought good results in my riding. Some 30 per cent of the lobster fishermen have taken insurance; you may think that this figure is very small, but, as a matter of fact, it is the largest figure obtained in all Canada. I am told that among fishermen, those on Magdalen islands have been the most num-
Supply-Fisheries
erous to avail themselves of this insurance. On the other hand, I have heard it said that the possibility of abolishing this kind of insurance may be considered in view of the small number of fishermen who use it. I wish to warn the department against such a step, because I believe that this insurance act affords a valuable service and that with a little advertising among fishermen in other parts of the province of Quebec and the maritimes, it would be possible eventually to convince them of the necessity of this insurance.
I was pleased to hear the hon. minister state that fish consumption was increasing and I congratulate him as well as his department. I am positive that this increase is the result of the enlightened efforts made last year to popularize the consumption of fish. As a matter of fact, we have had the opportunity to appreciate the efforts made by the Department of Fisheries when we were invited to relish the delicious dishes prepared with the products of our fisheries. I want to mention, not only the meal then served to us, but also the new recipes given to our housekeepers. I know that some of these recipes were given to the wives of our members of parliament and some of my colleagues have confessed that the results were simply marvellous. I congratulate the minister and his department and I hope that they will continue to popularize the consumption of fish.
Mr. Chairman, in order to encourage such consumption, to provide further education for the fishermen and to foster modernization in general, I submit that larger amounts should be spent on education, the opening up of markets and the political economy of the Department of Fisheries. I note with surprise that the amounts for those items have decreased somewhat this year. In my opinion, such savings are not wise; they will not give satisfactory results. I submit the amounts should have been increased rather than decreased, in order to open up new markets and help the work of the department.
Now, I read with satisfaction in the minister's speech-I do not know whether it was in last year's speech or in the one he made this year because I read both-about the investigation work he has ordered, to find new fishing banks or new scallop beds. Scallops are quite popular and there is reason to believe that if more intense research were done, new scallop beds would be found in

Supply-Fisheries
the gulf of St. Lawrence, as well as other herring banks; we know that there are large quantities in the gulf of St. Lawrence, but their exact location is not known.
While I am on the matter of the gulf of 3t. Lawrence, I would like to mention the problem of territorial waters. Several hon. members have referred to this matter and the minister himself spoke briefly on it, which shows that it is an important problem. I believe that Canada, at the United Nations and elsewhere, should insist on the settlement of that matter of vital importance for our fishermen and should demand that the limit of territorial waters be set at at least 12 miles.
In this connection, may I suggest that Canada should insist that all the waters of the gulf of St. Lawrence be considered as Canadian territorial waters. A line should be drawn from the southwestern tip of Newfoundland to Cape Breton and it should be laid down that within this line all waters are to be Canadian territorial waters. After all, the gulf of St. Lawrence is surrounded by Canadian territory and we would be justified, I think, to designate that part of the gulf of St. Lawrence as Canadian territorial waters reserved to the fishermen of this country.
I could not bring these remarks to a close, Mr. Chairman, without returning to the subject of unemployment insurance for fishermen. The house knows that ever since I have been sitting here I have unceasingly attempted to obtain unemployment insurance for the fisherman. Last year I managed to have myself temporarily named to the committee on industrial relations and to have adopted by this committee a very precise recommendation according to the terms of which the house was requested to extend unemployment insurance benefits to fishermen, as quickly as possible. It was even recommended that salaried fishermen be immediately allowed to come under this act, and that the question of what could be done for the others should be left for later consideration. I know that it is not under the direct jurisdiction of the Minister of Fisheries, but it is a matter in which fishermen are interested and I feel sure the Minister of Fisheries will look into it actively. It is to be hoped that this situation will not last too long a time and that we shall soon see practical results.
Mr. Chairman, may I suggest that there should be closer co-operation between the Department of Fisheries, the Department of Transport and the Department of Public

Works, which I often have to approach to obtain the construction of harbours and breakwaters. It seems to me that, if the Department of Fisheries saw fit to give us its support, we would be a little more successful, and that is why I suggest greater co-operation between those departments.
Incidentally, I take this opportunity to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Fisheries to the urgency of digging a channel at Oyster bay and of putting up a breakwater at Grosse Isle North and another one at Havre aux Maisons as well as at Anse Milterand, Anse a la Cafoane and Anse au Ruisseau. A breakwater would be a great help to the fishermen of those three localities. We also need a breakwater at Premier Etang. Once again, I lay before the hon. Minister of Fisheries these requests from the fishermen of the Magdalen Islands and ask him to make every effort to have those works undertaken as soon as possible in the interest of the fishermen.
In conclusion, I once more congratulate the hon. Minister of Fisheries on the remarkable way he got over his injuries and wish him, on behalf of my electors of Magdalen Islands, a complete recovery as soon as possible.
