Mr. Chairman, I wish to express the good wishes of this group to the Minister of Fisheries who is back with us once again and looking well. I sincerely hope that no further complications set in and that he will continue to take his usual place and look after his department, as he has so ably done in the past.
This morning the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam indicated he hoped that some further expenditures would be made on wharves and that the minister would talk to the Minister of Public Works to see whether or not something could be done in that way. I would like to echo those sentiments because in my riding there have been a number of instances where from time to time fishermen have found it difficult to get their boats to the wharves owing to dredging that needs to be done on the Fraser river.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam did make a statement which I am sure he did not expect me to pass by without comment. He said: "The federal government may find the provincial government making a deal that will completely frustrate the good intentions of the minister." He was referring to the building of power dams on the Fraser river. I should like to assure the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam that he need not

have any fear along that line. I am sure he should be satisfied by now that there is no man who has the interest of British Columbia industry-and the fisheries industry is one of those, and a major one, I might say-at heart so much as has the premier of British Columbia. I believe the Minister of Fisheries himself made reference to that when he spoke last Friday, although it was not my privilege to be present to hear him. He said, as reported at page 1751 of Hansard:
The provincial government has also been most helpful. They have announced that no licences will be granted on the Fraser river for a power dam until the problem of the movement of fish has been solved.
I am sure that if the Minister of Fisheries is satisfied that the provincial government of British Columbia will not hinder our fishing industry, certainly the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam should take that as evidence that nothing will take place in that regard.
Before carrying on with the text of my comments, I wish to thank the hon. member for Fraser Valley for taking my part in the debate the other day when the minister first spoke; but I must say there is a certain advantage in speaking at this time. I have had the opportunity to discover what the minister himself had to say on certain questions and the advantage of knowing that many of the questions I would have asked have already been answered. This gives me the opportunity to revise my remarks in the hope that I shall not be repetitious in the debate.
There is one thing that should be emphasized, though, and it has been brought out particularly by several hon. members, including the hon. member for Fraser Valley, who asked that unemployment insurance be made available to the fishermen. I know this does not come under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Fisheries, but he should use his influence, as he has in the past, to try to get a greater number of fishermen under the terms of the act. It is a fallacy to say that no fishermen are under the act, because certain part-time fishermen who do qualify for part-time insurance are entitled to it and they are getting unemployment insurance at this time provided that they fall within the group that was taken care of under section 119 as revised by the Minister of Labour earlier. However, I am satisfied that the minister is cognizant of the fact that this provision is not sufficient in itself, and that ' section 45(2) should be changed, or its complete deletion should be striven for at this time.
I feel that it would be to the advantage of the fishermen themselves and the Department of Labour if it were made possible to
Supply-Fisheries
extend the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act to cover a certain section of the country to which I shall refer later. I think an effort should be made to see whether or not it would be feasible to make these workmen recipients under the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act, with slight modifications, of course.
There is one matter which I think I should mention and that is the co-operation I have always experienced in my dealings with the Department of Fisheries and the minister of that department. I must say it is one department which sends out information bulletins regularly and I seem to get my share of them. If I have ever required information I have never failed to get it; all I have to do is ask for it, although I must admit that I sometimes find it a little difficult to reconcile what appears to be conflicting information. I shall refer to that more specifically in a short while.
One of these bulletins interested me very much. I do not think the minister touched upon this matter and he might wish to comment on it later. I refer to the December 1 issue of a bulletin issued by his department through the office of Mr. Campbell. This has to do with the progress report of the fishermen's indemnity fund. It says:
Benefits under the fund were increased in British Columbia in December, 1954, when the basis of payment of total loss claims was increased from 60 per cent to 70 per cent of the appraised value of the vessel. At the same time the deductible percentage was lowered from 30 per cent to 15 per cent.
Both of these factors are important and highly commendable.
There was one factor in the report, however, that did give me some concern and that is the fact that certain areas were not paying their way, one might say. I do not wish it to be construed that I am suggesting each area should pay its own way because insurance does not work on that premise. However, I found it interesting to note that of the boats that were insured, British Columbia stood highest in the group; the value was much higher in British Columbia than in any other province. At the same time British Columbia was the only province which made a profit; something like $32,694. Each of the other provinces lost money; an over-all deficit of $28,807. The bulletin does say, however, and this is very important:
It should be pointed out that losses on the Atlantic coast have been unduly severe as a result of two hurricanes: one in 1954 and one in 1955.
I was hoping the minister would comment on that matter, but not specifically on the monetary loss. More particularly I hoped

Supply-Fisheries
he would comment on the loss of life in connection with the losses of vessels. I am satisfied that too many people in Canada today have the impression that fishing is a pretty easy way of life for a man and I would like the minister to comment on that. If no loss of life has occurred in this connection possibly the minister could give us an indication of the loss of life of fishermen at sea.
I mentioned earlier that the reports I received gave me considerable concern because they did not appear to agree in some instances.
I have here a report dated February 9 which was also issued by the Vancouver office of the Department of Fisheries concerning salmon spawning. I intend to read just one paragraph from the first page:
Outstanding feature was the failure of the chum run to almost every section of the coast. Immediately evidence of this condition could be perceived, drastic conservation measures by special and early close-down of net fishing operations were applied. The run proved to be not more than one third of normal and definitely was the lightest return in the history of the fishery. Despite the drastic regulatory restrictions-
I would like the minister to comment on that phrase, "despite the drastic regulatory restrictions".
-the escapement for reproduction purposes was, with few exceptions, exceedingly light, and with present information the situation definitely will require special conservation measures four years hence in an effort to rehabilitate this particular cycle. The spawning escapement of the cycle year 1951 was such that a normal run was to be expected; and because of its coastwide character it can only be assumed that the failure was the result of very unfavourable survival conditions either in the fresh water or later during existence in the ocean of the progeny of the 1951 brood year.
I would ask the minister to comment on that particularly because during the past two years it has been the privilege of the hon. member for Fraser Valley and myself to draw to his attention certain changes he proposed in the regulations with respect to closures on the Fraser river. I should like to again repeat the question the hon. member for Fraser Valley asked the minister earlier. Does the minister feel that the closure of the Fraser river above the Westminster bridge is the answer to the problem? I am satisfied that he will have had sufficient opportunity by this time to have studied this problem at great length. That is the question which I think requires an answer. If closure is not the answer to the question, I wonder if the minister would consider ia modification of his earlier proposals made in the past two years.
There are other questions that enter into the subject of conservation in which I am vitally interested. I wonder if the minister could define for us the number of fish that

were caught by gill netters in the season during which the river was open for fishing above Westminster bridge in former years as compared with this year and last year, let us say, in order that we may have a more complete picture. I am not aware whether or not the department differentiates between the number of fish which gill netters and seiners catch, but in view of the fact that such a conservation scheme is in effect and because there was such violent opposition to it in past years, I think the fishermen are entitled to know what change has taken place in the net result. I think, too, that we are entitled to this information.
In his address the minister touched on the question of fish caught in Pacific waters, but that is another matter with which I wish to deal. As I understand it, as a result of the meeting at Tokyo a certain understanding was reached with the Japanese and United States fishermen. I wonder if the minister could bring us up to date on this particular question and tell us what has transpired since that time.
In view of the minister's visit to the U.S.S.R., at which time he was unfortunate enough to have experienced an accident, I would ask him to comment on what view we hold towards U.S.S.R. and what their view is towards us in relation to fishing practices and what is proposed to be done about the matter. I raise this question because I notice that the fishing vessel owners' association recently intimated their desire for equality of catch between gill netters and seiners, if r properly interpret the account set forth in the February 1956 bulletin of the association.
I said earlier that reports form the Department of Fisheries conflicted with what certain other parties had in mind. One thing that has come to my attention particularly, in respect to a matter that gives us great concern and also causes great concern on the Pacific coast, is mentioned in the fisheries magazine and has been mentioned in many other bulletins issued by the department, that is the flood conditions that take place on the Pacific coast in the spawning area, which virtually wiped out some 60,000 pinks and 30,000 early chum salmon in the Chehalis river. That was not the only river affected. The report states:
The Chilliwack river system including the Vedder river suffered less disastrous results, but even here losses of up to 50 per cent of pink and early chum spawning will likely materialize.
The gravity of this situation cannot be overemphasized. We cannot have fish if we do not have the spawn to begin with. If they happen to die en route, it is just as bad if they die as the result of excessive rainfall as

if they go over the top of the dam. So I should like the minister to comment on that phase and relate it, as he is so capable of doing, to the question the hon. member for Fraser Valley raised with respect to the bulldozer helping the fish to return home to spawn.
There is another point in the same article from which the hon. member for Fraser Valley quoted. It is the following:
Even though the Fraser river is navigable for fish for hundreds of miles, there are comparatively few places which salmon choose for their spawning grounds.
In one of the other articles, we find a notation that on the Capilano and Indian rivers, because of the forest cover along the rivers, the spawn were not lost to the same degree as along the Chehalis, where the trees have been taken away from the mountain. Because we realize that the spawning grounds are not so plentiful, I was wondering whether any thought had been given to conserving the woods of those areas where we do not have the fish spawning, and having those particular areas kept wooded at all times so they will not suffer from excessive wash coming down the mountainside.
There is a conflict in the reports, however, in regard to the fact that a certain Vancouver publication-I believe the Vancouver Sun-mentioned the precarious position of the coho salmon spawning and in this instance the fisheries report-and it was part of the same one that I mentioned earlier-made reference to that on the 9th of the month. I received a follow-up from the minister's office explaining the complete story, in so far as the public was concerned at least. It was indicated that the coho situation really was not too bad. It took the northern coast, for instance, from Smith inlet north to the Alaskan boundary, including the Queen Charlotte islands, and it said that the spawning generally was satisfactory. It said that in the Butedale area the seeding showed a marked decline and in the lower Queen Charlotte islands it was light. In the Vancouver island area, it said that some areas fared better than others. Then, breaking that down, it said:
Alert bay area, Cowichan area and Kyuquot area were above average. Pender Harbour was satisfactory; Quathiaski and Comox fairly good, but less than the brood years. Barkley sound, Nootka, Quatsino areas were light. Nanaimo was very light. In the Fraser river system, however, several of the areas showed a marked increase over the brood years.
This is very interesting in view of the fact that we have this statement made by apparently responsible individuals outside the
Supply-Fisheries
organization itself who went into the coho situation. It goes on:
These included Kamloops, Yale-Merritt and the Mission-Harrison and Chilliwack. Unfortunately a good early seeding in the lower sections of the Fraser suffered extensive damage from the phenomenal rainfall in early November and resulting flood conditions.
Breaking that down into areas, I find there were five areas. One was satisfactory, which I consider to be a normal year. I do not know whether or not my definition of the term "satisfactory" is proper, but that is what the minister's department calls it, and I should think that is in order. One area showed a marked decline. Another was light. Then there was the statement that some areas fared better than others. I find only one of those indicated as being satisfactory. In the group about which it is stated that some areas fared better than others, only one is satisfactory and all the others range from light, fairly good, and less than the brood years, to very light. I would not call that whole area satisfactory, under those circumstances.
Then there was another area with a marked increase over the brood years. That was the last area I mentioned, in the Fraser river system. However, from the earlier report I read to you in respect to the area that was flooded, I find that the Chilliwack region, the Harrison lake region and the Pitt river region were all in that area-one-half of the area, actually-and the spawn there was from 50 per cent to 90 per cent lost. That would indicate, then, if my analysis of the situation is right-and probably the minister can show me where I am wrong, because he has all the facts and figures at his command-that we are not warranted in suggesting to the fishermen that we do not face a serious condition in so far as the elimination of our cohoe fishery is concerned. I am somewhat concerned about that.
Possibly my conclusion may be wrong, but I think we should be privileged to get more information from the minister on this. I should like to ask the minister to comment on this aspect in view of the fact that there seems to be a notion abroad among the fishermen that there is a confidential report that has not been made public with respect to this matter. I am not accusing the minister or his department of withholding information. I just think we have the right to know, and I shall look forward to hearing his reply to that particular question.
There is just one other item with which I wish to deal at this time. I intend to spend more time on the power dam situation and its effect on the fisheries on another occasion,

Supply-Fisheries
but now I turn to a release from the dominion bureau of statistics in its daily bulletin of Monday, 6th February. It is headed:
Catch of Sea-fish Down Nine Per Cent In Volume and Ten Per Cent In Value In 1955.
It goes on to say:
Canadian sea-fishermen landed nine per cent less fish in 1955 than in the preceding year and the value of the catch fell about ten per cent.
Here again we have a primary, industry that is losing some of its cash returns. It is somewhat different from the agricultural situation. Here it is not a matter of surplus, but we have a difficulty in catching sufficient fish to keep our stocks, as we would like them, at a maximum. In his address, the hon. member for Fraser Valley mentioned that we are pleased that we do not have a surplus of fish on hand and we are able to get rid of our stocks and our canned supplies. I do not necessarily agree with that point of view. I always like to have a few cases of things on hand just in the event of next year not being too good. In this instance it would not help the fishermen in any event because they would not get any greater cash return. However, the fact of the matter remains that as one who was in the grocery business for many years and saw my customers denied the right to buy a tin of sockeye salmon I feel that a few *cases of sockeye kept on hand are not going to hurt at all. We should not have too much difficulty disposing of them. Let us not make it too much of a practice.
In the next paragraph I find the following with respect to the declines:
In 1955 the values of all three major Pacific fisheries declined appreciably from their 1954 levels: salmon by 22 per cent . . . halibut by 38 per cent . . . and herring by 9 per cent . . .
I believe those are the three chief fisheries of the Pacific coast and as such they are bound to have their effect on so many people not only in my community but also in the community of the Minister of Fisheries. For that reason I think we should put greater and greater emphasis on the need of a greater degree of co-ordination and co-operation between the minister's department, the Department of Labour, the Department of Public Works and every other department that might have anything to do with the matter in order that these people may continue to get as big a return as possible from their investment. The fishing vessel owners association have indicated that they feel they have some responsibility to the gillnetters and I believe the department should also realize that it is not only the fishing vessel owners who are faced with a problem with respect to the gillnetters which they want to resolve but that the department also has a duty in this regard.

If conservation does not bring about an improvement over the situation we had a couple years ago then, while I do not necessarily say that it is necessary to go back to that situation, we should determine means whereby we can be sure of having a supply of salmon each year.
There is no object in protesting, as the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam did, about dams and so on if we have no fishing industry to protect. The objective is to have a fishing industry. Maybe the answer should be to let the fish go up the river and spawn first and then go out and catch all we want to afterwards.

Mr. Chairman, I too should like to congratulate the minister on his speedy recovery from his serious accident and assure him that all members welcome him back to the house. The manner in which he presented his statement when these estimates came before the committee indicated very clearly, I believe, that the Minister of Fisheries has great knowledge of his department which is of great value to those interested in the fishing industry.
During the short time the minister has headed the department a great many improvements have been made which the fishermen perhaps had expected over the years but concerning which no action was taken until recently. In that regard I refer to the fishermen's insurance plan which was introduced a short time ago. Obviously it was practically impossible for the fisherman to insure his fishing boat. The rates charged by the average insurance company made it prohibitive. With the plan now in effect almost any fisherman can insure his boat, which to him is his bread and butter. The rates being charged by the department are most reasonable, and at the same time I believe that the losses are very small. The insurance plan is a sound plan, and I can assure the minister that the fishermen in the area from which I come appreciate this very much.
Only last year a plan was introduced whereby those engaged in the salt fish industry were assisted. The federal government undertook to be responsible for 50 per cent of the cost of salt. There again I wish to assure the minister and the officials of his department that this was a move in the right direction and one which is appreciated. Not only is the contribution of 50 per cent of the cost of the salt beneficial to the fishermen but the fact is that many fishermen have been encouraged to salt their own catch. Previously they would sell their catch for 2, 3, or 4 cents a pound, but when this plan was introduced many of them decided to salt a greater portion of their

catch themselves, which means greater revenue to the fishermen. The fishermen of the area from which I come are most appreciative of this action on the part of the government.
The fishermen's indemnity act which went into effect a short time ago has not, of course, been in operation for a sufficient time to find out just what benefits the fishermen may expect. I realize that the banks in the maritime provinces have not had any experience with this type of loan in the way that western banks have had with the farm loan act. Therefore it will perhaps be some time before the scheme is organized properly, but I do hope that it will provide the assistance for fishermen for which it was intended. I am sure that over a period of time it can be worked out in such a way that it will be of benefit to all fishermen.
Another matter I wish to mention briefly is the kitchen over in the west block. In the past two or three years I have attended two or three luncheons there, and I believe that all those taking part in that organization deserve a great deal of credit. I must say at this point that in the ten or eleven years I have been here there has been a great improvement in the serving of fish in the city of Ottawa. The fish served today is far better than two years ago, five years ago or ten years ago. I believe the fisheries department should receive some credit for the improvement. The kitchen in the west block should be maintained and expanded, if possible.
I noticed in a pamphlet put out by the fisheries council a few days ago, which I had intended to bring with me, it was stated that in the city of Toronto and other places they had been given a great deal of encouragement to carry on this type of informational and educational work in connection with the fishing industry. It has always been my belief that in order for our fish to take the place they should take with the consumers of this country we must continue to produce a better article in a fresher state and see that it is cooked properly. I feel that the great disadvantage we have had throughout the whole country has been the fact that those who would have liked to have fish in their homes were not given any information as to how it should be prepared.
Until the last few years, in many cases they got fish which was not fresh and once it had been served they were not satisfied with that particular type and did not buy it a second time. With the facilities we have today for bringing fresh fish to our cities where the great bulk of the population is, I believe that every encouragement should be given the industry to produce a better article, get it in the homes and keep it there. I know
Supply-Fisheries
that encouragement is being given the industry by the fisheries department and the biological board, and I believe we are doing a very good job in that regard at the present time.
The fishermen in the maritime provinces also appreciate the accelerated effort by the department in the important field of research. They are doing a very fine job which I know is appreciated by all fishermen. Last fall I attended a meeting of officials of the fisheries department of this country, those of the United States and others connected with the industry at a place called Hinkley's Point in the state of Maine. It was one of the finest international gatherings I have ever attended. Each individual spoke very frankly. The main discussion at that time was a survey in connection with the herring and sardine fisheries on the Atlantic coast. I believe the officials of the two countries and those engaged in the canning industries of the two countries are of one mind. It is a fine thing to find the officials of the fisheries departments in these two countries ready and willing to sit down and work out these problems together, in co-operation. It will save a great deal of repetition as a result of one country doing the same work as the other one is doing. When I found that type of co-operation there, I was convinced that the survey will be a success. I know that the departments are extremely anxious that it be carried on. I have discussed with the minister a similar survey which was conducted on the Pacific coast a few years ago. According to reports that we received from that section of the country it was most successful, most advantageous to the industry and most advantageous to the department. We shall be pleased to see that type of investigation carried on on the Atlantic coastline.
By other hon. members who have already spoken mention has been made of the serious shortage of clams in that area. We all realize that the clam industry has never been a great producer of wealth. At the same time it was an industry that employed a goodly number of persons during the winter months when dollars were not too plentiful. I agree that the situation today is serious. At the same time I believe that the green crab which has infested our waters in that area during the past few years may be to a great extent responsible for the situation. Then again, the great improvement in the prices which were paid to the producers has encouraged a much greater number to be employed in that industry. I know the department is doing everything possible to try to find some answer to the problem. I hope they may be able to come up with something which may be helpful.

Supply-Fisheries
Only a few weeks ago-I believe it would be seven or eight weeks ago now-I was at the biological station in St. Andrews. At that time they put on a film strip which portrayed the dragging of scallops. I have mentioned this matter to the minister. In my opinion it was one of the finest types of work that the department could ever hope to produce which would be helpful to those engaged in the industry. The way in which the light from the ship was regulated on a sled behind the drags made it possible to sit and watch the scallops being dragged off the ocean bottom. It gave a clear picture of the way that the drags might be improved. I myself have dragged some scallops. With the information provided by this film strip I know that I could today devise a drag that would drag more scallops than those I used a few years ago. Work of that type is most helpful to the industry; it is most interesting to the industry and it means dollars to those engaged in it. We have not the scallop fishing they have in Digby and over that way, but our scallop fishing this past winter has been encouraging enough that we have had with us at least two or three boats from Digby dragging in Charlotte county area waters this winter. I trust the department will continue with this type of work because it will be found that it pays dividends and is most helpful to those engaged in the industry.
I also wish to say that the information compiled by the biological board in St. Andrews -and I take it for granted that the same is true with regard to the other stations-has always been made available to the industry. They have always tried in every way to be helpful and to encourage those who are trying to produce a better product. We have in the little town from which I come the largest exporter of lobsters perhaps on the North American continent. The assistance it has been able to obtain from the biological board has been most helpful. As a result, within the last few years, tanks have been installed in many of the larger restaurants in different parts of the United States to which fresh lobsters are shipped. They are kept alive in glass tanks. Those who come there and who like to have a lobster dinner-the best food in the world-can go to the tank, pick out the lobsters they wish, have them cooked and served to them in that restaurant. The biological board are to a great extent responsible for that improvement. I believe it will be of great assistance in building up this industry and in creating a greater demand for this wonderful food.
At the present time lobsters are being transported by trucks from the Conley lobster plant in St. Andrews as far as Florida. They

are making weekly trips with live lobsters from St. Andrews to Florida. This is something which indicates clearly that even though the lobster is a most perishable article, with the proper facilities it can be placed in the restaurants and in the homes of a great portion of the population of this continent.
I have one suggestion to make in this regard. Conley's Lobsters Limited at one time owned a small lobster pound on the small island, namely Banes island which is in the Deer island area. When their business began to grow it became necessary to find larger quarters. This small pound was abandoned and has not been used for several years. The officials of the company assure me that that pound could be placed at the disposal of the biological board at any time they might wish to take it over for purposes of experimentation. I believe the matter should be looked into carefully. I am still one of those who believe that this industry can be helped greatly by looking after our spawn and small lobsters. I should like to see the department take an interest in this pound, which I know can be taken over without any cost to the department other than that of the personnel who look after it. The experiments that could be carried on there would be carried on in a place where the fishermen themselves could see them. I believe the benefits that might come from such experiments would be worth while.
I have just one bit of criticism to offer. During the past year the seining regulations in connection with the sardine industry were changed by the department. At the outset I wish to say that I did not oppose that change. I was opposed to it but a great number felt that it was an experiment which should be tried for one year. For that reason I did not oppose it. However, I was of the opinion that it would be harmful to those who are operating sardine weirs in the area, and I am still of that opinion. Nevertheless, it was carried on during the year 1955. I received a great many protests from fishermen all over the Passamaquoddy bay area. I do not think for a minute that it is the quantity of fish they oatch that is harmful. It is the commotion that goes on all night in the areas where these weirs are built that is harmful. I am going to suggest to the minister to give serious consideration to giving these fishermen 1,500 feet or 2,000 feet protection instead of 1,000 feet. With 1,000 feet protection from a sardine weir, with this work going on all night, the commotion is most harmful. Those who build weirs place them in one particular spot and are obliged to wait until the fish

come to them. I believe this is one matter that should be given serious thought.
I was informed today-and I am not in a position to state whether or not this information is correct-that with respect to sardines that were on the north shore-that is the area between what is known as White Head or Bliss harbour and point Lepreau, a school of sardines has been there since last December. Purse seiners have been in the area all winter. They have been able to provide the canneries in that part of the county with good supplies-nearly a daily supply of sardines. This fact is very much appreciated by those working in the canneries and who were unable to work last summer owing to scarcity. This has provided a very good income for those engaged in purse seining. I do believe that that school of fish has pretty well left the north shore at this time. The report I got this morning was to the effect they had found sardines in the Passamaquoddy bay area and the seiners were in there.
I did not communicate with the minister because the house met early this morning but at one time the regulations we had governing the area in which purse seiners were allowed to operate was from White Head, near Bliss harbour not including the St. Andrews bay area to point Lepreau. The seiners were not allowed to go inside St. Andrews bay. If purse seiners are operating in St. Andrews bay today I know the telegrams, telephone calls and letters I may expect in volume. I really believe that it should be stopped. There are sardine weir fishermen in the Passamaquoddy bay area right now who are preparing their weirs for spring. There is great expense in connection with these preparations, and I do believe they should be protected. Again I would say it is not the quantity of fish that the seiners will get in that area, but it is the breaking up of the schools of herring. They may be difficult to find after the seiners have been amongst them for a few weeks.
This letter I received today is from a fisherman who has been engaged in the industry for 35 years to my knowledge. He pointed out what we may expect, and in his letter today the forecast he made has proven true. There were large schools on this north shore during December, January and part of February, but the catch during these last few days has been practically nil. Now, in my humble opinion the seiners have not caught 5 per cent of the fish that were there; I do not argue that. As I have said, it is not the quantity that they catch but it is the commotion and traffic through the places where they stay winter after winter that does the damage. I might repeat what has been
Supply-Fisheries
said to me on many occasions, that 85 per cent of the sardine fishermen are opposed to this. Again, as I stated earlier, hundreds of people have been employed in these canneries who needed the employment. It is very difficult to strike a balance and know just where to draw the line; no one realizes that more than I do. I spent several winters on that coastline in this very type of work. I realize that those who go out in the winter months to make their bread and butter on this coastline earn all they get. But the feeling is very strong in connection with purse seining, and in the opinion of a great many it breaks up the schools of fish so that when spring comes it is impossible to find them anywhere. This is a very serious matter.
Years ago the sardine fishermen in the area from Pocologan down the north shore to Bliss harbour, Back bay, Deer island in St. Andrews bay area, depended to a great extent on the spring school of herring for a great portion of their annual income. During the last few years we have not had a spring school of herring, and as I have said many believe it is the winter seiner who is responsible for it. I have not any idea myself other than I know that, before the winter seining was introduced, somewhere in the area I have mentioned we would get that spring school of fish. At that time of year stocks were usually sold out and the price was as a rule better in the spring than any other time of the year. If this regulation with regard to that area is still in effect and it is open for purse seining, I would ask the minister to look into this very carefully. The school that was on the north shore has been broken up. If there is a school of sardines, as I am informed, already in the St. Andrews bay area and the purse seiners break them up again and there are no sardines in the spring, we are all open to a great deal of criticism.
There is another matter that I want to mention and it was brought out by the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Van Horne). He mentioned the serious situation with regard to the salmon industry on the rivers of the province. It would appear from his remarks and the remarks of many others that this great industry is being neglected by the federal fisheries department. I have heard this same criticism in the house directed to the federal government in connection with conservation of our forests, our streams and so on. I do not want any member of the house to think for one minute I am blaming one government more than any other, because in my lifetime we have had different provincial governments in my province. In this house I have always

Supply-Fisheries
been critical of any provincial government which will allow our raw materials to be exploited and then come to the federal government for aid. For many many years these salmon pools on our rivers have been put up for auction and sold to millionaires from outside our country. This has happened under both Liberal and Conservative governments. Our own citizens have been denied the right to fish in the pools on these rivers. However, mention is never made of the fact that the federal government provides the personnel to protect these rivers, yet every dollar of revenue from licences of any kind or from the sale of the pools goes into the provincial treasury. I believe that before too much criticism is aimed at the federal government in this regard we should clean house in our own province. Before I am accused of making a political speech, which is usually the accusation I receive, I want to say that I have said this when we had Liberal governments in my province and I say it today when we have a Tory government.
More so now.

And not any more now; I have spoken on the same subject in this house on different occasions. I do not believe it is right for any provincial government to allow their crown lands, their fisheries or any other resource of this country which belongs to the people of the country to be exploited by citizens in that province, and then come to the federal government asking for assistance and condemning the federal government for not playing their part. I believe we have the power in our own province to start conservation measures. Now, I will resume my seat because I have taken more time than I intended. I know the minister will give these matters I have brought to his attention serious consideration. I know his health will improve and he will be able to carry on and do the same type of job as he has done since he came here as Minister of Fisheries.

I would like to take this opportunity, and I am sure all other hon. members in the house join me, of saying how glad I am to see the minister back in his seat and looking so well after his unfortunate accident. You know, Mr. Chairman, there is an old saying that if you tell a man often enough he is looking sick, eventually he will get sick. I think perhaps after the first item of the minister's estimates is completed that saying will work in reverse and if there is any recovery still necessary it will be completed by the time the minister's estimates are finished.

It may seem very strange to hon. members from the maritimes or British Columbia that a member from central Canada should have any remarks to make about fisheries. However, as the minister and his staff well know, and I hope many other hon. members know, the fishing industry on the great lakes is of very considerable value. In the report of the minister's department it says that the sale value of fish from the great lakes was aproximately $8 million, a little bit less, but almost $8 million. Now, the fishing industry on lake Erie, and lake Huron particularly, not only provides a source of income but it employs many persons. It is a particularly valuable industry because the bulk of the fish caught in those lakes goes to the United States and provides us with United States dollars which, because of our present balance of trade with that country, are very valuable indeed.
As I have already mentioned, this industry is very valuable and its value can be increased, although in the last few years, as hon. members know, because of the lamprey eel and other things, the fishing industry has certainly dropped off in the great lakes area. It is our hope that it will revive, increase in value and employ more people.
A fisherman's life on the great lakes is a pretty healthy one. In my younger days, when I was going to school, I used to spend a great deal of each summer visiting and sometimes working on the fish boats going out of Port Dover, which is in the constituency of the hon. member for Norfolk. Port Dover, as some hon. members may know, is the largest inland fishing port in the world. At the present time there are 25 or 30 modern diesel tugs operating out of this port. I am sure the minister and his staff are aware of this, and I do not wish to take any further time dealing with facts which they already know.
When the great St. Lawrence seaway project is completed in a couple of years a couple of problems which are now in existence will become increasingly important. These two problems will certainly have an effect on the fish population of the great lakes, particularly of lake Erie. These two problems are, firstly, the danger of animal and plant life from the ocean, which are not indigenous to fresh water, getting into the lakes and upsetting the balance of nature and possibly causing considerable harm.
With regard to the first matter, I should like to refer hon. members to what happened with respect to the lamprey eel. As far as I have been able to understand it, the lamprey eel may well have been in lake

Ontario for many thousands of years because, apart from the international rapids and the Lachine rapids, there was nothing to prevent them from getting into lake Ontario. However, Niagara falls was too much of a barrier even for the lamprey eel, and it never got into lake Erie and subsequently lake Huron and lake Superior until there was some other means of passage. Apparently the means of passage was provided by the Welland canal. Well, the Welland canal is of varying size and depth. It has been in existence for well over 100 years. First, there was a 7-foot draft canal, and then a 14-foot draft canal, and now we shall have a 27-foot draft canal. Despite the earlier canals, apparently the lampreys were never noticed in lake Erie until 1921. It is my understanding that lampreys got into lake Ontario by riding-I was going to say "piggy-back", but perhaps I should say "piggy-bottom"; that may be a better term-or sticking to the bottom of boats and going through the lakes. There is a possibility they may have been getting through the locks as they were being filled up from time to time. My colleague, the hon. member for Lambton West, dealt with this problem this morning. Lampreys have caused great depredations in the fish population of the great lakes, particularly lake trout. I understand they are now starting in on the whitefish. This should teach us a little lesson.
The Minister of Fisheries is certainly to be highly commended on the lead he has given in efforts to control and get rid of the lamprey eel. I am very glad to see that an additional $130,000 is included in the estimates this year for that purpose. If we succeed in controlling and eventually getting rid of the lamprey eel we certainly do not want them coming in from the ocean again once we have got rid of those we already have. After the construction of the St. Lawrence seaway project it might be advisable for the minister, if he has not already done so, to take steps to make sure that some type of screening process takes place to prevent, not only more lampreys from getting up into the lakes, but also other forms of undesirable ocean life. The minister may very well say: It has not come in so far. Maybe it will not come in, but after the St. Lawrence seaway is completed we shall have a 27-foot canal, almost double the present depth. There will be a great increase in shipping on the great lakes. At the present time most of our foreign ships come from Norway, Sweden and Holland. With the increased depth of the seaway we will probably have ships from all over the world which will have various things sticking to their hulls. It may be well for the minister, as I said before, to take
Supply-Fisheries
some precautions to prevent undesirable marine life, both plant and animal, from getting into the lakes on the bottoms of ships or swimming into those much larger and much deeper locks.
While the Welland canal has been in existence for over 100 years, in one way or another, yet the lampreys never got into lake Erie in any quantity until 1921, and did not cause serious damage until the late 1930's. In this regard I should like to make a couple of suggestions to the minister. First of all, I think the great lakes fisheries research committee should investigate the possibility of placing new types of ocean fish in the lakes. This is a sort of procedure the reverse of what I have already mentioned. We have had one very good example of that in the great lakes, namely, the great lakes smelts. The smelt, as hon. members from the maritime provinces know, is a very small edible fish. Smelts in the great lakes have provided a valuable source of fish food and, I may say, pleasure to individuals who go smelting in the springtime. As I understand it, smelt got into the great lakes from a small lake in Michigan which was stocked with those fish. They came down a small stream into lake Michigan and spread around. That is one explanation I have heard; there may be others. As I say, these smelts have provided a very valuable source of food and pleasure to the residents around the great lakes. It may be that other forms of ocean fish could be put into the great lakes that would survive under fresh water conditions and would not upset the present fish population, and might in fact increase, give employment and cause us to sell more fish as well. This is just a suggestion. It may be that the research committee is looking into this matter. I hope it is. If it is not, I hope it will take this hint.
When the lampreys are controlled-and we have had various estimates of the time it will take-I hope the minister's department will take the lead in making attempts to rehabilitate the great lakes with lake trout and with other forms of fresh water fish. This will probably be done by the provincial authorities, but an additional subsidy from the federal government might be very helpful.
I mentioned before-and I repeat it because I do think it is important-that once the seaway is completed, and before it is completed, some plan, some arrangement for screening the Welland canal in particular should be put into effect to prevent the lampreys at least from getting back into the lakes once they are controlled.
The second matter I would like to deal with is pollution in the great lakes, and in

Supply-Fisheries
lake Erie in particular. I mention lake Erie because it is a very shallow lake. I believe the average depth is around 70 feet, if my memory serves me. The deepest spot in the whole lake is only 190 feet, and it is at the end of Long Point island. In this regard, I should like to refer to a clipping from the Sentinel-Review of Woodstock, Ontario, dated Friday, March 2, 1956. I shall read just a portion of the clipping. The heading is:
Welland health director says Erie being polluted.
The paragraph reads as follows:
Dr. L. W. C. Sturgeon, director of the Welland county health unit, told the Ontario pollution board Thursday lake Erie is becoming more contaminated every year.
We have an abundant supply of good water from lake Erie, but the drainage problem in the Welland and Port Colborne areas is complicated by the abundance of heavy clay.
Dr. Sturgeon said new types of virus diseases are being encountered, such as a mild outbreak of jaundice in one district school last year.
I mention this in passing because it illustrates the desirability of looking into this matter of pollution. Pollution of necessity consists of two types. There is pollution by sewage, which is, of course, animal or vegetable waste matter which eventually would dissipate. In fact, in some cases, it might even form a type of food for some of the fish of the lakes.
The other type of pollution is caused by chemicals, and it would tend to be cumulative in effect. I refer to the type of pollution that might very well be caused by ships blowing off once a day, cleaning their bunkers of oil which goes all through the water. Hon. members know that our beaches along the Atlantic coast have been spoiled because of oil collecting on the beaches and in the water. This might have a very serious effect on the fish life of the great lakes. With the greatly increased shipping that will come with the completion of the St. Lawrence seaway, with certain chemicals being used for cleaning the decks and the holds of ships and that type of thing, this waste will be dumped in the lakes and it might have accumulative effect.
If we look far enough into the future, ships eventually might very well be powered by nuclear energy and their waste products might be dumped into the lakes unless steps are taken at this time to control this type of action. Not only will the fish life in the great lakes be endangered, but the water which may be used for municipal purposes in the states adjoining the great lakes and also in Ontario will be polluted. If pollution is allowed to accumulate in lake Huron and lake Erie it will not only kill the fish but

will present serious problems to these municipalities which will have to use this water in the immediate future.
I know this does not come under the heading of fisheries exactly, so I shall not pursue it further, but I did want to mention it in passing in order to show that the increase in traffic on the great lakes which will come as the result of the seaway will increase the possibility of pollution.
I should like now to refer to the remarks of the Hon. Lionel Chevrier who, as all hon. members know, is the head of the St. Lawrence seaway project. I wish to refer briefly to some statements he made when speaking about potential traffic on the seaway in an address he gave in Copenhagen, Denmark, on May 20, 1955:
Estimates of the traffic which will utilize the seaway in the years immediately following its completion suggest a total of 30-35 million tons of cargo per year. This may be compared with approximately ten million tons currently passing through the St. Lawrence canals.
He goes on further to say:
Overseas trade was pioneered by Norwegian interests in 1933, it expanded sporadically in the years before world war II, but was discontinued during the hostilities. Re-established in 1945, this trade has since expanded at a phenomenal rate.
By 1954, the total volume exceeded 780,000 tons and involved 14 shipping lines and 120 vessels. It is worth noting as a measure of growth that the number of shipping lines involved doubled between 1952 and 1954. This has been accomplished it must be remembered, despite the handicaps of the existing 14-foot canals.
Referring to future traffic in foreign shipping, Mr. Chevrier had this to say:
Estimates vary considerably, but there is substantial reason to believe that the present volume of this traffic (over one-half million tons) -
That is, foreign shipping coming from abroad.
-will be more than treble in the years immediately following completion of the seaway.
... It could be expanded some 25 times its current level without exceeding the tonnage of similar traffic now handled by ports in comparable U.S. coastal districts.
I mention this because Mr. Chevrier is, as I think all hon. members will agree, the leading authority on the St. Lawrence seaway project and its potentialities in this country and perhaps elsewhere as well. I think these figures should not be taken lightly by any means. The shipping and the pollution, which are already rapidly growing on the great lakes, will continue to grow at a great rate with the completion of the seaway. The problem of waste materials being dumped from ships and the problem of sewage disposal in the lakes will also increase. In deep lakes like lake Huron it may be a long time before the effect is felt, but in shallow lakes such as lake Superior, from which comes the

bulk of fish from the great lakes at the present time, the effect will soon present a problem to municipalities.
In this regard I have a suggestion which I hope the minister might consider. I suggest the setting up of a joint commission with the United States to control pollution of the great lakes. If such a commission were set up it could investigate the present sewage pollution problem and the chemical pollution problem and other factors, and could endeavour to estimate what damage if any, future pollution might cause. It might be that pollution would not be found to be a serious matter, but it would appear serious to me. This commission could investigate the type of pollution that is likely to occur in the great lakes in the foreseeable future, the amount of such pollution and the effect, if any, on the fish population.
If such a commission were set up I think particular attention should be paid to the cumulative effect of chemical pollution particularly by oil and chemicals being dumped into the lakes. If the commission were to decide that a serious problem could develop in future as the result of increased pollution, steps could be taken to control pollution before it takes place, before it destroys the fish life and renders the waters of the great lakes unliveable for the fish and unusable for the human population in the surrounding area.
There is no point in shutting the barn door after the horse is stolen. If vision and foresight had been used in the past we would not have the lamprey problem today. I feel that the Minister of Fisheries and the officials of his department have both foresight and vision. I suggest to the minister that the setting up of such a commission to study the volume of anticipated pollution and its effects should be borne in mind, and it would be my hope that the department would do something about it before it is too late.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to make a few remarks under this general item. First, however, I wish to state briefly, but nonetheless sincerely, that I am sure we are all pleased to see the minister well on the way to complete recovery.
All phases of fisheries have been discussed since this item was brought forward; therefore my remarks today will be limited. On the whole the Department of Fisheries is making good progress. The status of the department as a component part of government continues to rise, which is a good omen for the future of the industry.
The peculiar habits of the different species of fish, the divergent views on international
Supply-Fisheries
fisheries, and the limited number of qualified biological and research workers available, are only a few of the problems that have to be faced. These are problems which I contend cannot be solved over night. Advances have been made in all branches of the department, new and improved legislation and regulations have been introduced over the years, all of which is encouraging and beneficial to the industry. Broad statements have been made about the inefficiency of the department and its officials. Statements have been made to the effect that there is a serious decline in fisheries. None of these statements has any foundation in fact.
At this point, Mr. Chairman, I wish to place a few facts on record. The 25th annual report of the Department of Fisheries for the year 1954-55, on page 55, gives a general review of the fishing industry which I feel should be placed in part on the record for the information of those who have not read the report:
Canadian fishermen generally enjoyed a satisfactory year in 1954. Total landings of fish and fish products amounted to slightly over 2.0 billion pounds compared with approximately 1-85 billion in 1953. Much of this increase was attributable to substantially heavier landings of cod and haddock, in the Atlantic area. In addition British Columbia's herring fishermen recorded their first full calendar year production since 1951.
Average returns, with few exceptions, compared favourably with those of 1953. Gross landed value totalled approximately $97-7 million as against $90-2 million and the marketed value of the year's production is estimated at close to $185 million as compared with $174-2 million in 1953.
The total value of exports reached a record $132-6 million.
To those who are interested in fisheries, I suggest that they read this annual report. I am sure they will agree that the scope of the department's work is very extensive and the results obtained have been very good.
The 1955 annual report of the New Brunswick department of industry and development, fisheries branch, states in part on pages 12 and 13:
New Brunswick's sea and inland commercial fisheries reached a total of 212,450,000 pounds of fish and shellfish for a landed value of $7,186,900 during the calendar year 1954. In comparison with 1953 this represents an increase of 9-4 per cent in quantity and 5 per cent in value.
How, then, does anyone justify the statement that New Brunswick fisheries are in serious decline?
In regard to species of fish caught in the world-renowned Miramichi river, which runs through the riding of Northumberland-Miramichi, such as salmon, -smelts, oysters, lobsters and other varieties of fish-all of which are delicacies-I shall make a few comments when the particular item comes before the committee.

Supply-Fisheries
I wish to say a few words on a matter that has been the subject of much discussion inside and outside this house; that is, unemployment insurance benefits for fishermen. I realize the difficulties that are faced in the working out of a plan to embrace fishermen, owing chiefly to the fact that the majority of fishermen are self-employed.
I do not need to remind the members of this house that of all occupations fishing is the most strenuous and hazardous and, as far as the east coast fishing is concerned, the industry with the smallest financial return to the individual. The majority of Atlantic provinces fishermen find it extremely difficult to eke out an existence. They are at the mercy of the elements, and many of them spend their entire lives in the fishing industry, with very little to show for a lifetime of endeavour, through no fault of their own.
There are no better Canadians than the east coast fishermen. They carry on under all sorts of adverse conditions. They do not come begging to parliament when they have a crop failure, or a loss of boats and gear caused by storms, and they -have never witnessed a crop surplus. These hardy fishermen go back to the sea with faith and courage to recoup their losses by their own efforts. They are to be commended for their spirit. It is unfortunate that some of this admirable spirit is not shown by another group, in another part of Canada. It would have a splendid effect on the present and future morale of our country.
These east coast fishermen know and appreciate that the Minister of Fisheries and the Minister of Labour, whose department administers the Unemployment Insurance Act, are exploring every avenue with a view to enacting legislation that will make fishermen eligible for unemployment insurance benefits, or some other plan that will provide assistance during periods of unemployment. I know the matter is receiving most serious consideration by the two ministers and their officials. I trust that a solution will be found in the near future to provide these benefits for this group, which is so deserving of this advantage now enjoyed by most Canadians, particularly in view of the adverse conditions they must face -conditions beyond their control-which make the provision of a livelihood an almost insurmountable task.
In the matter of protection, much is heard on the east coast of New Brunswick about illegal fishing of lobsters and salmon. I think there has been a definite improvement in late years. However, I feel that additional protective services would benefit the lobster and salmon fisheries. Salmon fishing associations,

both commercial and sports fishing, have requested additional protection, particularly in the spawning areas.
At this point I should like to say a word about the dates for east coast salmon fishing. As a conservation measure the date was set ahead last year to June 5. This date was arrived at after a recommendation was received by the department from the Atlantic salmon co-ordinating committee. This was the first time all the Atlantic provinces, including Quebec, agreed upon an opening date. This date was concurred in by the department after all factors were considered, and the recommendation was put into effect, strictly as a conservation measure. It is generally felt that it was a necessary step; and when the records are compiled after the trial cycle period, the department will be in a better position to assess the future of the east coast salmon fisheries.
In closing, I wish to ask the minister if he has anything to report on the research that is being done in connection with the possibility of spawning the early run salmon at our hatcheries. I also wish to ask him if he will arrange for the showing of the films on the life and habits of the lobster to the Miramichi lobster fishermen at an early date, prior to the opening of the season in area 7B.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Like other members who have spoken, I should like to extend my congratulations to the Minister of Fisheries on his restoration to good health. I am also happy to join in congratulating him on the excellence of his administration of the Department of Fisheries. I have been pleased to note some of the innovations that have taken place during the period he has been minister, including the fishermen's indemnity plan, as well as other steps he has taken to improve the lot of those engaged in this industry.
I should like to join with the previous speaker and others who have spoken in this debate and express the hope that, along with the Minister of Labour, it will not be long until he will find a way in which to bring fishermen under the coverage of the Unemployment Insurance Act.
However, my purpose in rising at this time is to say a few words not merely because of an ancestral interest in fishing but because I happen to be a member of a group that is extremely important to the fishing industry. I refer to the consumers of Canada. I join with the member for Charlotte in congratulating the department on what it has done in its kitchen over in the west block and on what it has done generally in its consumer services. But it does seem to me, Mr. Chairman, that there is still room for a great deal

to be done by way of research, publicity and education with regard to the cooking of fish.
I do not know of any food that can be more delectable than fish when it is properly cooked. The opposite is also true. I do not know of anything I would rather stay away from than fish when it is not properly cooked. We can find examples of both extremes in this city, but I think the words of the hon. member for Charlotte were well spoken when he said that due to the work that has been done by the department there has been a noticeable improvement in the preparation of fish in Ottawa during the past few years.
When one starts to talk about the cooking of fish he realizes he is getting very close to the activities of the housewives of the country, and he must be very careful. I have in mind not so much the cooking of fish in homes but the cooking of fish in restaurants, cafeterias and other public places across the country. I feel very strongly that there is room for improvement there and I should like to make one or two suggestions to the minister.
We know, of course, of the kitchen that his department has in the west block and of the work that is done there, but I feel that the benefits and advantages of that study and work might be much more widely disseminated throughout the country. I wonder whether there has been any attempt at liaison or co-operation with the nutrition division of the Department of National Health and Welfare. I am glad to see the minister nod his head in assent. When I mention the word "nutrition" I think it will be clear that I have in mind not only the desirability of fish being a delight to the taste. I have the notion that there must be a tremendous amount of nutritional value in fish which is lost because in a great many places it is not properly cooked. I believe, therefore, that not only would it be good for the industry to do some educating in this field, but it would also be good for the health of the Canadian people generally if steps were taken so that the full nutritional value of fish were made available to all our people.
As the minister and other members of the house will know, the Department of National Welfare is at the present time conducting a survey amongst Ottawa civil servants to determine whether or not they are eating adequate breakfasts. I think such a survey is a very good idea, but I suggest that if it is possible to conduct a survey of that kind among a selected group of people, surveys might be made to determine the nutritional value of fish cooked in one way or fish cooked in another.

Kippers for breakfast.
