speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
My good friend the hon. member for Royal says that kippers should be provided for breakfast for all civil servants in Ottawa. I have no objection to that, but if so I think the project will have to be extended and a good meal of lake Winnipeg goldeye will have to be provided at some other time of the day. However, I am not going to pursue that today. I was led into it by my good friend from Royal. What I was starting to say was that I think it would be worth while for some department of government, or perhaps through liaison among several departments, to conduct surveys to ascertain the nutritional value of fish and then take whatever steps are possible to make the advantages of such a survey known to our people.
There are various ways in which the advantages of research into the proper cooking of fish could be disseminated. There are a number of departments of government which are responsible for feeding a great many people. For example, I think of the Department of National Defence. There is also the Department of Veterans Affairs with its veterans' hospitals. There is the Canadian National Railways, which provides a great many meals, and there are a great many government departments that have restaurants, dining rooms and cafeterias.
In addition, Mr. Chairman, if some new ways can be found of making sure that the goodness that is in fish is always retained when it is cooked, another way in which that knowledge could be distributed throughout the country would be, I suggest, by placing it in the hands of the provincial departments of education. I do not want to raise any constitutional issue here through the fact that the provinces have control of education, but recognizing that principle I think the provincial departments of education, under many of which instruction is given in what is called home economics, domestic science or cooking, would be glad to have that information so it could be passed on to the young people who are taking these courses in our schools throughout the country.
One of the things that must be said about the Canadian housewife as a good cook is that she is always ready for new ideas, and if the department would take steps to spread such new ideas by means of publicity of various kinds I think that would be most acceptable. I recognize that the minister's department has prepared some very interesting booklets already. We have all seen and had the privilege of sending to some of our frienas and constituents that well set up little

Supply-Fisheries
book on the cooking of fish. Perhaps that particular book is a little along the highbrow line.
It was very simple.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Maybe my hon. friend and I are thinking of different books. I think something a little more proletarian might have wider acceptance.
We have a good selection for all heights of brows.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is fine. I believe I have made my point. The minister appreciates the fact that these suggestions are offered in the spirit of trying to be helpful. I think it would be good for the industry. More fish would be sold if this kind of information were spread abroad, and I think it would be good for the health of the people of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, the compliments that have been paid to the minister and his staff have been well merited, but perhaps they would not be worth very much unless they were backed up by the fishermen themselves. I believe the sentiments of the fishermen were very well expressed last Friday by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth -Clare. I merely want to add that what that hon. member said is also true of every fishing village in Halifax county.
The work of the Department of Fisheries is well and concisely laid out in the 25th annual report of the department, which is the 85th annual fisheries report of the government of Canada. There is ample evidence there of the good work the Department of Fisheries is doing, and in that I want to include not only the minister, his parliamentary assistant and all the officials in Ottawa but all the fisheries officials who are stationed in the outposts, and I suppose I might include Halifax as one of the outposts. We have always found them very co-operative.
I might mention a few of the ways in which we are benefiting greatly and concerning which there is such a decided improvement. The first is the boat insurance which the fishermen have taken advantage of and which has been of great benefit to them. Then there is the lobster pot or lobster trap insurance which in particular has helped the fisherman, for it has given him a real opportunity to fish in places to which he might not otherwise go because of the danger not only to his traps but to himself. As everyone knows, lobster fishing is a very dangerous occupation. Then there is the salt subsidy which was very helpful to fishermen throughout the country, particularly in the more inaccessible places. They appreciate it to the full.

Last year we were pleased with what happened. I do not think it was perhaps necessary for the government to go out of its way to investigate this matter and voluntarily do what it did, but it returned the customs and excise duty to the companies which had paid these taxes when they brought ships into the country. Speaking for these companies I may say that I know they fully appreciate the work that is done. In this debate it has been said that St. Margaret's bay was cut off from trawlers and draggers at a time when perhaps votes were needed. I just want to say here that was not the case at all. I wanted to say at that time, if I had been able to do so, that when we do something we do it for the fishermen, not for the sake of the votes.
Then when home recently I saw on the street a shopmobile, a large trailer in which the federal government, working with the provincial government, are giving our fishermen an opportunity to repair and maintain their engines and motors.
There are perhaps three or four things that I might suggest should be done. I remember that when I was a young person in the country we had a number of lobster factories, and each village had what they call a lobster pound or lobster car in which the lobsters were kept waiting for the boats to call for them or for a time when the price might be a little bit better. It struck me that possibly there might be some assistance given to these country fishermen.
Last Friday I was pleasantly surprised to learn from the minister that last year the export lobster catch was valued at $16,714,000. This, it seems, was three times the value of fresh and frozen salmon exports.
On the east coast.
On the east coast. I have a note here that, of course, British Columbia canned salmon export was over $16 million.
How much?

Over $16 million. Another suggestion I should like to make is this. In going around the country I see some extremely careless handling of fish just as, when you go to the Annapolis valley, you see careless handling of apples.
Except in the Okanagan valley.

The situation must have changed since wartime. I wish that all officials at all levels, when they are visiting these various places, could go to these wharves and give the men instruction on how to handle fish. You see them throwing

them out on the wharves, or forking them out. This procedure just ruins the fish. Fish should be handled just as though they were the most delicate piece of china.
Then of course we are always asking for wharves, breakwaters and shelters. While this matter is not entirely in the sphere of the Department of Fisheries, through them I think the fishermen can be helped because even if there are only two fishermen in a small village, it probably means that 10 or 12 people are dependent on those fishermen. These people cannot go anywhere else and find employment. They must stick to their last there.
In travelling around the country, every one of us has seen how fish can be ruined in so many of our hotels. I wish that your dietitians, who do such a wonderful job in your own department, could visit these hotels and tell them that the best halibut is not improved by frying it or broiling it in tomato sauce.
Then as another suggestion I would hope your department would continue its efforts to stabilize the United States market. After all, I believe they take half our Canadian fish products. Every day I know you are receiving demands for further research. I am glad to read that there is now some possibility that lobster shells will be utilized. I know that your Halifax biological station has been working on this matter for some time, and I know that if anyone can find some further use for them, they will be able to do so.
I would draw to the attention of the minister the fact that in Nova Scotia clams seem to be decreasing in number and in some places going away entirely. I should like to mention one or two places, namely Musquodoboit harbour and Ostrea lake. At one time there were two factories in that vicinity. I think now we have one working only part time. They have to go many miles-I suppose up to 100 miles-to get their clams. I am glad to hear that your department is now working on this matter and has a machine in that area and will continue it down into Guysborough county. Perhaps the reason clams die and disappear from some places might be the subject of an investigation that could be made by our maritime universities. I would not mention any special one, but they could work in co-operation with your own biological station.

Mr. Chairman, I suppose some hon. members are wondering what I would have to say about fish, living as I do up in the interior of British Columbia. But of course that is where the important spawning 67509-126J
Supply-Fisheries
grounds of the salmon are. We have about 300 miles of the Fraser river in my riding. This river, with its tributaries, contributes a great deal to the fishing industry.
My reason for rising at this time is just to make one or two observations in respect of the rumblings of the battle that is shaping up as between fish and power. I should like to say that the fishermen certainly have a good case for keeping the fishing industry alive, in that they are producing food. When we consider the great populations of the world that are without sufficient food, we cannot but realize that the fishing industry is extremely important.
The thing I had in mind is this. I have read the statement of the minister at page 1920 of Hansard, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Kamloops, in which he said in effect that no permit woud be given for power dams until certain conditions had been met which were laid down by his department. The thing I should like to say is this. If by any chance a dam cannot be built on the Fraser river to provide power for the interior of British Columbia, I feel that we have an alternative in the use of gas which will be coming down from Fort St. John. There might be a slight difference in the cost factor of hydroelectric power and thermoelectric power.
If a block is to be put in the way of building a dam because it cannot provide a way for the fish to reach the spawning ground- that is, if it is decided that we cannot build the dam-and if the authority which is in charge of that particular phase of the fishing industry says it is in the interests of Canada that the dam should not be built, then I feel that compensation should be given so that the cost of thermoelectric power in that area should be no more than it would be for hydroelectric power.
I feel that we must get power in that area very soon. I realize that engineers are now working on plans to see if they cannot provide some way for the fish to get up to the spawning grounds and the young fish to get back again. I am hoping that if we do find we cannot build a dam there to supply the people of the interior with power, consideration will be given to making the thermoelectric power just as cheap as the hydroelectric power would be. I do not feel the people of the interior should be asked to subsidize the fishing industry. I believe we must keep the fishing industry alive, and there may not be too great a difference between the cost of thermoelectric power and hydroelectric power. If there is some difference, I believe it should be taken care of by some sort of subsidy.

Supply-Fisheries

May I point out to the hon. member that the new government did not
Supply-Fisheries
take over the day after the election; it was some days after. They do not change immediately.

I might tell the hon. member that the fishermen were aware then there would be no objection from the provincial government, in trying to protect the interests of the inshore fishermen. Once again, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that those inshore fishermen must be protected, and it might be advisable to enforce, by regulations, the gentlemen's agreement which existed up to September, 1952, in connection with certain sections of the bay of Chaleur.
May I ask the hon. member a question? Does he not know that the federal government, not the provincial government, has control of trawlers?

Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member had been listening he would have heard that I said this was done by a gentlemen's agreement, and that representations were made to the federal government to protect the waters of the bay of Chaleur. I might also inform the hon. member that the deputy minister of the department of industry and development and the director of fisheries of New Brunswick were here in Ottawa in January-I think it was January 15, 1953-and made representations to the Department of Fisheries against the protection of the waters of the bay of Chaleur for inshore fishermen.
Yes; again I want to keep the record straight. This was in 1953. The hon. member said the day after the new government of New Brunswick was elected. That was in 1952, not 1953.
Again I want to make clear to the hon. member that after September 22, 1952, there was no one in New Brunswick to protect the interests of the inshore fishermen.
Where was the Minister of Fisheries?
The Minister of Fisheries received recommendations from the fisheries division of the department of industry and development of New Brunswick.
You are just trying to talk politics.

During the course of the debate on the fisheries estimates last year I brought to the attention of the house the situation of the herring fishermen on the Atlantic coast. Again I want to mention at this time that our herring fishermen are still using the same outmoded and inefficient methods adopted over a century ago. Would the minister advise the house as to whether

Supply-Fisheries
the Atlantic herring investigation committee, which was operated as a joint effort of the government of Canada, the government of Newfoundland before that province entered confederation, and the provincial governments of the maritime provinces and Quebec, has completed its investigation, and if a report has since been published, as this committee, I understand, was dissolved in 1950.
The herring fishery on the Atlantic coast has reached an importance which calls for full consideration by the fisheries research board and the government. Our fall run of herring in the gulf of St. Lawrence waters is considered to be of the best quality available, and is comparable to any production of its kind originating in any European countries. It is generally recognized that the herring resources of the Atlantic coast are not fully used. If new fishing methods have been discovered by the fisheries research board these methods, if practical, should be made known and made available to the individual fishermen. Further efforts should be made to develop a method of catching herring which could be made adaptable to the large number of inshore fishermen all along the coast of the maritime provinces and particularly in the gulf of St. Lawrence area. In New Brunswick alone in 1954 the herring catch exceeded 52 million pounds.
In the last 10 years additional herring plant facilities have been added in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and the demand for food purposes, as well as for the meal and oil industry, is increasing every year. A dependable source of supply, an extended fishing season, and more knowledge of the characteristics of herring populations have become necessities if we want this particular phase of the industry to expand as it really should. Much greater developments in this industry are possible, and I ask the minister to assure us that every effort will be made in order to carry on with, the initial surveys, undertaken in the last three years, for the success and benefit of this particular industry.
New Brunswick, with its 30-odd varieties of fish and shellfish, and a total production of close to 200 million pounds of fish a year, is a heavy producer of oysters. Gloucester county alone produced in 1955 over 11,000 barrels of this delicacy, or one-third of the total production of oysters in the maritime provinces. This particular fishery, which is well established in certain areas of my constituency, depends largely on research work and on special methods of production and conservation to meet its current problems and provide for further expansion.
The department, through its research board, has centred at Ellerslie, Prince Edward Island,
[Mr. Robichaud.l
its activities in this respect. A substation for oyster research and for the study and application of methods of oyster culture has also been established at Shippigan. Last year in the course of my remarks I brought to the minister's attention the fact that the staff of the substation was being reduced, and that very little is being done there to revive this gradually vanishing industry. Unless proper conservation methods are enforced and new production methods are introduced, the declining yield which has been so evident in other areas could easily extend to Gloucester county.
We now have in the oyster-producing areas of the maritime provinces a total of about
1.500	oyster leases covering approximately
3.500	acres. A good portion of these leases, or privately-owned oyster farms, are located in my constituency of Gloucester. Again, Mr. Chairman, I urge the minister to increase the staff at the Shippigan substation in order to carry out further investigations to improve the position of the oyster industry in the area. Collection of spats and test-planting should be done on a much larger scale. I even suggest that one of the scientists from the Ellerslie experimental station be stationed at Shippigan for the summer months' in order to direct on the spot an activated and more elaborate survey of the situation. Additional help is available locally, and an educational program should be launched without delay to introduce lease-owners to practical methods of spat collection and oyster farming.
In this respect, I do ask the department to have, sometime in late April or early May, a demonstration course at Maisonnette, an area where oyster farming is being done on a large scale. I look forward to this course in April or May of this year.
Last year the department saw fit to change the minimum length of oysters for market from 3J to 3 inches. This measure has resulted in an unusual increase in production in certain areas, and furthermore has had an adverse effect on consumer market conditions in central Canada. If such a measure had to be introduced for the benefit of the industry, a reduction of one-quarter of an inch the first year would have been advisable and would have prevented a glut of small oysters on the market which resulted in a substantial reduction in prices paid to fishermen.
An oyster committee appointed by the Montreal fish merchants' association has protested vigorously against this measure, and is seriously disturbed and annoyed over the fact that the firms in Montreal dealing in oysters were not consulted before such a change in regulations was adopted. They are not concerned mainly over the additional

quantity of oysters involved, but rather by the large percentage of small oysters which are being offered the market.
Another change in regulation which could be very detrimental to the oyster industry is the introduction of an early season in many parts of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. Under the new regulations oyster fishing is permissible on private leases from August 15. Any one familiar with the oyster industry and with weather conditions in the maritimes should know that the temperature of the water at that time of the year is such that it is not advisable to remove any quantity of oysters from their natural bed. It is true that the fishermen do not have to rake the oysters as from August 15 and offer them for market. The opening of a season, however, is an incentive or an inducement to lease owners to participate at once in the revenue which they may expect from the harvest of their oyster crops.
As a result, oysters which are just about over the spawning period and are still feeding heavily are removed from water at a temperature in the vicinity of 60 degrees Fahrenheit and are transported to markets in Montreal or Toronto in outside temperatures ranging from 60 to 75 degrees. Oysters in very poor condition are delivered and offered for sale, and these could easily affect market conditions for the entire season. If the owners of oyster leases as well as public-bed oyster fishermen were consulted, I am convinced that an overwhelming majority would oppose the opening of the season before September 15 for private leases and September 25 for public beds.
Mr. Chairman, I would suggest to the Minister of Fisheries that a survey be made in this respect by officials of his department in order to give the whole matter the attention and consideration it deserves. I sincerely hope that the activities of the research board in this field will be accentuated, and that every possible effort will be made to increase the availability of seed stock for seeding and planting purposes.
It is generally recognized that companies and individual fishermen engaged in harvesting fishery resources cannot control or regulate the source of their raw material. It is therefore the responsibility of the government to conduct necessary research, impose conservation regulations and negotiate when necessary with foreign countries on controls to perpetuate stocks. We realize that oceans do not lend themselves readily to scientific study, and that progress in fishery research will be slower than similar experimentation with land crops or any agricultural product.
Supply-Fisheries
We welcome an increase of 25 per cent in the amount provided in the estimates for the fisheries research board. This is a move in the right direction which will meet with the approval of the primary producer as well as management in the industry. I %urge the government to provide the minister with a sufficient appropriation to maintain an efficient organization for carrying out federal policies and regulations, such as inspection of plants and products and all other activities pertaining to the development and future of the industry.
The presence of fish, of an adequate supply of raw material, alone is not sufficient to maintain a healthy industry operating on sound and solid principles. The primary producer, whose fishing occupation is a way of life, must be assured that his remuneration will provide a very important share of his family cash income. In order to give this assurance, the fish processor and buyer should be in a position to keep their prices at a level which will enable the fisherman to meet his obligations. It is the responsibility of the government to see to it that both domestic and export markets are supplied with quality products which will gradually increase consumption and provide necessary outlets to take care of increasing production.
If we take for example the cod fishermen or the flounder fishermen, we find as the result of economic surveys that a landed price of at least 3 cents per pound must be paid for his catch in the fresh state in order to provide sufficient income or revenue to meet his obligations and for him to maintain a reasonable standard of living in comparison with other classes of society.
As we make provisions to protect the dairy farmer in regard to his butter, the wheat grower in regard to his wheat, the labour class by unemployment insurance and fair wages, the civil servant by security and pension funds, we must also find means of protecting the fisherman by assuring him of a minimum price on certain commodities of fish. As cod fishing is the basic occupation of the large majority of full-time commercial fishermen on the Atlantic coast, I suggest that a minimum price of 3 cents per pound should be obtained for this particular variety.
However, under existing conditions with rigid inspection, careful processing and packaging, together with well planned marketing, it is possible with the co-operation of all concerned, including the primary producer, the industry and the government, to assure the cod fisherman of an adequate and satisfactory return for his production without having to introduce a floor price or some kind of assistance or subsidy.

Supply-Fisheries
Mr. Chairman, I want to emphasize once more the need for the continuation of an educational program and a well-prepared publicity campaign to prevent the unfortunate practice of illegal fishing among lobster fishermen. In the last three years tremendous progress fias been accomplished in this field, and all branches of the department concerned must be congratulated for the results obtained. I wish to assure the minister that we are looking forward to a continuation and further expansion of this educational policy.
I would suggest, however, that more consideration be given to the large number of fishermen on the east coast of New Brunswick whose only language is French and by whom instructions in any other language cannot be properly understood. I would suggest that more use of the press be made for publicity and educational purposes, including French daily newspapers whose circulation is very popular in most French speaking fishing communities on the New Brunswick east coast.
I was amazed to learn that the Halifax office had notified the department that no French posters and no application forms in French were required for Gloucester county fishermen in connection with the rebate applicable to salt used by fishermen in the processing and curing of certain varieties of fish. The department should be made aware of the fact that out of approximately 800 fishermen in Gloucester county 75 per cent, or approximately 600, are French speaking and cannot understand or speak any other language.
Mr. Chairman, with the consent of the house I could conclude in two or three minutes.

speechtext: Has the hon. member leave to proceed?
Agreed.

Thank you. Some members have made mention in this debate of the brief submitted to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects by the fisheries council of Canada. I agree that this brief is excellent and well prepared and covers many aspects which could face the fishing industry in years ahead. There are two recommendations, however, which I would approach with great caution.
First is the suggestion put forward that the government should consider the emigration of fishermen to Canada. Before acceding to this request I suggest that we should first consider the possibility of improving the situation of our own Canadian fishermen. We in the maritime provinces are complaining that our young men are deserting our industries for the central provinces. Before

considering increasing our fishing force with immigrants, let us first make this profession more attractive to our young generation; let us prepare them through proper education. Then and only then will we be in a position to keep in the maritimes the large number of young men who are now forced to move out in search of a better situation.
Another recommendation in this brief which I would approach with caution is the question of government control on vessel importation and the existing import duty on vessels up to 100 feet in length from most favoured nation countries. We have too many shipyards scattered all along our shores seeking business to hamper them further by allowing the duty-free importation of the type of vessels which they have been supplying the industry for many generations. The skill, ability and craftsmanship of our Canadian shipyard workers is so eminent that they should be given every opportunity to take full advantage of Canadian outlets for their products.
I am in full agreement with the remarks made with regard to bringing our fishermen under unemployment insurance benefits. I will reserve my observations on this subject until we consider the estimates of the Minister of Labour.

I wonder if I could have the indulgence of the committee for just a moment, since it is obvious that item 1 is not going to be carried today. First of all I should like to express my personal thanks for the many kind things said about my own health. I think the hon. member for Oxford put it very neatly when he said that with all these expressions of good wishes in regard to my health I certainly should feel much better.
I am also glad that for the first time the fishing members have had a chance to have the estimates of the Department of Fisheries first discussed. I think the participation of members from every part of Canada and from every party will show the fishermen of Canada that there is an increased interest in fisheries.
The other thing I should like to mention is the fact that quite a number of members have suggested that when I do reply I make some mention of my own experiences in the field of fisheries in the Scandinavian countries, in Russia and in China last summer. I do not think that would be quite appropriate in a discussion of the estimates of the Canadian Department of Fisheries, but I have written to the chairman of the standing committee on marine and fisheries informing him that, if it is the desire of that committee,

I will be very glad to appear before it and report on my experiences over there and be questioned by the members of that committee.
Progress reported.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stanley Knowles (Winnipeg North Centre) moved
speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 121, to amend the Canada Elections Act.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, as I indicated
when first reading was given to this bill, its purpose is to extend the privilege of voting at an advance poll in connection with a federal general election to any qualified voter who finds that he will be absent from his constituency on election day. As hon. members will have noticed, the bill consists of nine pages, and some may wonder if there is not more in the bill than is suggested by that simple explanation. The fact is that everything else in the bill is consequential upon the one change which is sought by the bill, namely, the extension of the privilege of voting at advance polls to all qualified electors who find they will be absent on election day.
I am sure that many, if not all, members in the house will agree with me that at least in urban areas the most common complaint at election time is that many voters who will be away on election day find that they cannot vote at 'the advance poll. This is particularly annoying to voters who are aware of the fact that there is such a thing as an advance poll and who discover that only a very limited group of people may vote at that advance poll.
As hon. members are aware, the privilege of voting at advance polls is restricted at the present time to commercial travellers, fishermen, persons employed upon railways, vessels, airships and so on, members of the reserve forces and of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. In recent years federal general elections have for the most part been held in the summer period and rumours are that the same will be true next time. In fact I understand that those who, like the Minister of Trade and Commerce, like to look into crystal balls when they are not out on loan are already guessing as between June 17 and June 24, 1957, for the next general election. At any rate, with elections coming in the summertime a great many people do find that they are away on holidays at election time.
Some people may find it possible to get back to their constituencies in order to vote but for many people this is either impossible because of the distance they have gone away from home or because of the cost involved. It seems to me, therefore, that it is a legitimate grievance that many people have, namely, that there exists an advance poll

but that many qualified voters do not have the right to vote at that advance poll. In my own province of Manitoba that grievance is felt very strongly at federal elections because the privilege of voting at advance polls is extended in provincial elections to all qualified voters who find they will be away from home.
I urge this amendment to the Canada Elections Act, Mr. Speaker, not only to meet a grievance which is often expressed by voters but because it seems to me that it implements a principle underlying the whole business of voting. In our democratic approach to these things we feel that people should be encouraged to vote, that every person who is qualified to vote should have it made possible for him to get to the polls and to cast his vote.
No one would suggest that a measure of this kind has any partisan motive, at least not so far as a member of an opposition party is concerned, for the fact is that if you go through the results of general elections you will find that generally speaking the winner in a constituency has also obtained the largest number of votes cast at any advance polls in his riding. In other words, although it is not a universal rule, those who vote at advance polls tend to vote in the same proportion as do the people who vote on the regular election day. Therefore in no sense is one advocating anything that is of partisan interest. Likewise, in no sense is one advocating a special privilege. Rather we are simply advocating that the principle of the universal franchise be implemented by the further extension proposed in the bill.
In addition to meeting a grievance and implementing a principle, I feel that taking this step would have the effect of removing a feeling of discrimination which does arise every time we have a federal general election. Those whose names are on the voters' lists, those who are qualified voters, who in turn discover that they cannot vote at an advance poll whereas certain groups of people can vote at those polls, feel that this is a form of discrimination. The reasons that people are obliged to be away from home on election day are many and varied. People feel that the attempt of any law-making body to decide which of those reasons are legitimate and which are not is practising a form of discrimination which is not consistent with the principle of universal suffrage.
There is another way in which people feel there is a form of discrimination. I have already alluded to it in my suggestion that some people who are away from home on election day can afford to get home in order to vote while others cannot afford to make such a trip. I therefore feel, Mr. Speaker,

that here is a chance to remove these feelings of discrimination with regard to voting at advance polls, and I urge the house to give serious consideration to this proposition.
As I have already indicated, it is generally thought that the election for the 23rd parliament of Canada will take place in 1957. One of my friends to my right wanted to put it off a year the last time I mentioned that date. But whether it is in 1957 or in 1958-

Toward that end I invite the house, particularly the members on the government side, to consider seriously and favourably the idea of approving this bill in principle by voting for it on second reading and letting it go to the committee on privileges and elections. With the number of details that are contained in this bill, it would obviously have to be gone over by a committee. If a matter like this is left until another year, it may not be implemented in time for the next election. In other words, Mr. Speaker, the time to deal with this matter is at this session, if we are going to remove the grievances to which I have referred and if we are going to implement the principle of the universal franchise to this extent in time for the next election.
Another reason for urging the house to approve the bill and let it go to committee is the necessity of looking at all the various clauses and all the various details in the bill. Purposely-not just because there is a rule against it-I am going to refrain from discussing any of the details of the bill. As I have already indicated, the bill calls for a number of changes which are consequential
Canada Elections Act
upon the primary change which is made so as to extend the privilege of voting to all qualified electors.
One of the changes involves putting the voting at advance polls on a different set of days than is at present the case. That change has been suggested so there may be a longer period between the voting at the advance polls and the voting on the general election day, in order to enable the various election officials to make the necessary deletions from the election lists and do all the other things that are necessary to make sure there will be no duplication of voting at the general election as a result of this change.
There are other changes that are made necessary, such as the date on which nominations would close and various details of that kind. If I were even to specify what those details are, I can well imagine that some hon. members would prefer one set of days rather than another for the advance poll voting. However, Mr. Speaker, that is not the point. The point at stake on second reading of this bill is this simple principle, namely that the right to vote at advance polls be extended to all qualified voters.
I have had occasion to mention a few of the details which it has been necessary to work out and incorporate in this bill. May I take this opportunity of expressing my thanks to two individuals-they are servants of this parliament rather than servants of the government-who have assisted me in drafting my bill. Those officials, as anyone would imagine from reading the bill, are, of course, our parliamentary counsel, Dr. Maurice Ollivier, and the chief electoral officer, Mr. Nelson Oastonguay. I wish to make it perfectly clear that my having mentioned their names does not mean that they are either for or against the principle of this bill; but their help, in order that I might draft a bill which would set forth the mechanics to carry out this principle, has been most valuable and I am grateful to them for their assistance.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, what is before the house is a bill-although it has details that some hon. members might like to alter a little here or there-that is more than just an abstract proposition. It is not just a pious resolution suggesting that it would be a good idea to have a wider extension of the privilege of voting at advance polls. Rather it is a bill that sets out the mechanics by means of which it can be done. On that basis I feel that the matter should receive the approval of the house and that the bill should be sent to a committee so it can be studied.
I would emphasize the point that the assistance I have received from the officials whom

Canada Elections Act I have named has enabled me to put in the bill appropriate clauses to provide against any additional corrupt practices at election time. As a matter of fact, I think it is fair to say that the necessity for that protection which results from extending this principle has resulted in producing mechanics toward this end that I believe are even better than those that are in the act at the present time.
There may be those who will feel that the exact terms of my bill extend this principle too widely. I do not think so. I do not think any law-making body, even parliament, should set itself up as the judge between two different reasons that two different persons may have for being away from home on election day. When you start to draw lines of that kind you can readily become unfair. That is the reason I have drawn my bill so as to make it possible for any person to have this privilege, provided he will take an affidavit to the effect that he has reason to believe that he will be absent on the ordinary polling day and that he will be unable to vote on that day in his own polling division.
You will note, Mr. Speaker, that my bill requires any person wishing to exercise this privilege to take an affidavit. It is true it is just an affidavit to the effect that he believes such and such to be the case. Nevertheless, I feel that is a sufficient safeguard so that the right to vote at the advance poll will not be abused. I feel that, too, because of our own experience in the province of Manitoba. We have had this universal right to vote at the advance poll for many years, and it has not been abused. In the main people still find that their interest is in voting on the general election day, and that is when they vote. The numbers who vote at the advance poll are really not very great.
Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, if some members feel that some point should be found between the present very severe restrictions which are in the act and the very wide provision that is set out in my bill, then of course that is the kind of detail we can discuss in committee and perhaps we can reach agreement on it if the bill is permitted to go to the committee on privileges and elections. I can say, as ministers often say when they are introducing bills and trying to win favour from the other side, that after second reading of this bill I will have pleasure in moving that it be referred to the standing committee on privileges and elections. I feel that a measure of this kind, though it might not affect a great many people, will nevertheless further our interest in the full practice of democracy. It will increase the interest of our people in voting at election time, and


I suggest that anything of this nature is all to the good at this stage in the history of democracy.
So, Mr. Speaker, I commend this bill to the consideration of the house. I hope there will be a fair amount of discussion on it during this debate on second reading, and that there will be an opportunity for members to learn what are the opinions of the people around the country. I was interested in noting that the Canadian Chamber of Commerce has already written to members of parliament urging that this bill be supported. I happen to know that various labour organizations of this country also support the principle of this bill, as indeed both the chamber of commerce and labour organizations have done for some time.
As I say, I hope the principle will be discussed by interested members representing all parties, and that when that discussion is over second reading will be approved by the house so the bill can go to the committee on privileges and elections where any amendments might be made, so that before the end of this session this change in the elections act might be upon our statute books.

maintopic: EXTENSION OF RIGHT TO VOTE AT ADVANCE POLLS
speechtext:
I
have listened with great interest to the remarks that have been made by the sponsor of this bill. As the minister responsible in parliament for the chief electoral officer, who administers our election act, I think I should say a few words to express my views on this proposal the result of which would produce, I think, a very serious, if not radical, change in our electoral legislation.
The hon. member has mentioned the interest of outside organizations such as the Canadian chamber of commerce as well as other chambers of commerce throughout the country, which have expressed the view that this bill ought to receive the support of the government. I have read those representations and I may say that they appear to be, as I am myself, in agreement with the principle of the proposal. However, I am sure that if they were to give careful study to the act as it now stands, and to the proposal that has been made, they might very well come to the conclusion they ought to change their views and should, as I am going to do, oppose the proposal now made by the hon. member.
I think everyone is in agreement with the principle. I have said so myself on a number of occasions. If we are to have a democracy which will produce as many of the beneficial objectives as possible, if we are to allow as free and general an expression of the will of the people as circumstances will permit, then we will all favour the principle underlined in

this bill. In other words, we will want to have as many Canadians as possible express their views on the choice of their representatives in this House of Commons. I am in agreement with the principle, but I think there are a number of reasons which, in my view, command us to be cautious in this matter and not go as far as the proposal which is made.
Under this bill the hon. member simply suggests that we ought to allow anyone, for any reason whatever, to cast his vote at an advance poll for the simple reason that he may be away from his polling division on polling day. In other words, all that would be needed to justify the establishment of an advance poll would be for someone to think he may be away on polling day and he would be allowed this privilege of voting at such a poll. As the act now stands provision is made to cover what I consider to be the exceptional cases, and those classes of people have been mentioned by my hon. friend. These classes include people who, by their occupation and not because of holidays or other reasons, cannot vote on election day.
I think if we were to go as far as my hon. friend would like us to go it would destroy the significance of polling day to the Canadian people. The whole machinery of the election act is prepared in order to allow an expression of opinion of the people on that one given day which is established and which is determined, even if my hon. friend would like to make predictions, by the government.
It is true that it is sometimes a little more difficult to exercise your right to vote during the summertime. It is true also that elections have been held during that period when holidays are being taken by the Canadian people. But I think under the proposal that is now being made, if we were to allow anyone who felt he might be away to cast his vote at an advance poll on the ninth and tenth day preceding the polling day, I would imagine a number of people would take advantage of that situation. It would tend to not only increase election costs, though that would be only every five years, but in the final result you would have established a new rule and the election day would not be the date for which the election was called.
This should be the only day upon which allowing for exceptions when they have to be made, the people of Canada will choose their administrators for the next years to come. Instead of that you would establish two other days upon which this would also be done. I do not think I would be exaggerating if I were to say that if this practice
Canada Elections Act
were established you might very well find that some day there would be more people voting at the advance polls than would be voting on election day.
I do not believe we want to allow this sort of thing to happen, for a good many reasons. Election day is fixed for a Monday. Nomination day is fixed 14 days ahead of that date, when candidates are chosen to conduct an electoral campaign. During that period of 14 days political parties expound their ideas. Candidates tell the people of Canada what they want to do to defend the interests and the rights of their constituents. During that period of time, which I believe is essential, the people make up their minds. I think that period of 14 days is essential to everyone who wants to exercise his right to vote with sound judgment. In other words this period of time, which is short enough in itself, should be completely allowed to the people of Canada in order that they may make a sound choice.
If we were to allow, as the proposal indicates, two other days to be considered also as polling days, we would find, I believe, that the significance and the importance of election day itself would be gradually reduced. I would not be surprised, in fact, to find that the interest of the people would be greatly reduced. By permitting many more people to vote at advance polls you would reduce the importance of the election itself. I believe the time would come when people would completely lose interest. We sometimes complain of the lack of interest of the public in elections. If anyone were allowed to consider that this privilege, this right, which is essential, could be exercised at his discretion on another day than polling day, then I believe you would certainly not serve the purpose that we have in. mind, which is to allow as free an expression as possible of the will of the people.
This question was considered last year in committee. There was a similar proposal by a member of the C.C.F. party. I read the minutes of evidence with care, and I believe the question received considerable attention by the members of the committee at that time. The proposal that was then submitted, and which was similar to the one we are now considering, was defeated by an imposing majority. Reasons other than the ones I have already mentioned were also brought forward.
Other reasons than those which I made known do also justify us in thinking that this measure should be opposed. There is the question of cost. We have been informed by the chief electoral officer that during the last election about 240 advance polls were established. The cost of these advance polls

Canada Elections Act
was about $100 each. The voters who availed themselves of the right to vote at those 240 advance polls numbered a little over 10,000. I have been informed by the chief electoral officer that if we were to accept the proposal made by the hon. member we would have to increase a number of advance polls considerably in both the rural and urban districts. It is his own feeling that it would necessitate the establishment of about one advance poll for every 15 polls in the urban districts, and one advance poll for every five polls already established in the rural districts.
The result would be, at the cost I have already mentioned, that it would require about $500,000 to take care of them all. I am not stating that this question of costs should in itself be considered as a very serious obstacle, provided of course that we would be able to obtain results which would be beneficial to the Canadian people. But I do not think such would be the case. If we were to establish too many of these advance polls, as I said before, interest would be lost in the election day itself.
As was mentioned in the committee last year, we would allow impersonation to take place to a greater extent than has happened in past elections, as a result of these advance polls being established. It would impose upon political parties the necessity of multiplying the number of agents in each of those advance polls. It would be very costly for political parties, and again it would not eliminate the danger of impersonation of electors.
Another important thing comes to my mind. There would be a period of nine days, according to the proposal we have here, during which the deputy returning officer would be in possession of the ballots cast. In other words, during that period of nine days an official, appointed, it is true, by the government in the person of the deputy returning officer, would have in his possession a great number of ballots-I believe the number would tend to increase at every election- that were cast at these advance polls. It would mean that during that period of time this man would be in a position to determine, not for whom the votes had been cast but what proportion of the votes that appeared on the electoral list had already been cast. It would mean that there would be a number of returning officers in those advance polls in Canada who would be able to say just what proportion of votes had already been cast and we would then be able to know during the nine days that remained, for instance, only 40 or 45 per cent of the electors had not yet cast their votes, so that the election would be of interest only to the remaining group of people in Canada.
[Mr. Pinard.l
I think that is a wrong principle. I am in favour of extending the right to vote to as many people as possible, but I believe this is a wrong approach. For all of these reasons I believe we should oppose this measure. We should oppose it because of the fact that it would reduce the importance of polling day itself; because it would increase the cost, and for that reason it would not benefit the country. Finally, it would render possible violations of the Canada Elections Act to a greater extent. For all these reasons I am going to oppose the measure.

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre had convinced me that his proposition was one to raise the percentage of votes in a general election, I would have been in favour of it; but he did not convince me that such a proposition would increase the percentage of votes in any general election.
My first reason for opposing it is that it would confuse the minds of the electors with respect to the propriety of casting their votes. We are all in favour of the principle of enlarging the right to vote, but in doing so we must bear in mind that the people of a democratic country are called upon to vote on a definite date, as was stated by the Secretary of State, and only those who cannot be in a position to cast their votes on that definite date are entitled to vote at an advance poll.
At the present time those who are given the right to vote at an advance poll are as follows, and I propose to read the explanatory note which is embodied in the bill:
The privilege of voting at an advance poll shall extend and shall extend only-
A list appears of the limited number of voters including commercial travellers, fishermen, and such persons as are employed upon railways, vessels, airships, members of the reserve units of the Canadian forces and members of the R.C.M.P., et al.
We know that by reason of their duties such people are not in a position to cast their votes on a definite polling date. I therefore consider that it is right to extend to them the right to vote on another date, but I am nevertheless opposing this bill very strongly,, especially in view of the clause which would extend the right to vote at an advance poll to anybody in any circumstances. This is the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre to section 95 of the elections act. This section reads as follows:

I think to do so would be to take another step in the wrong direction for a reason which I shall state. We are aware that it is extremely easy to find candidates for any general election. If we extend too much the period of time between the nomination date and the polling date it will be very difficult to find the right candidate to run in any riding in this country and I would think that enlarging the period of time is a bad move.
It would also increase the cost of elections. We find that a period of 16 days from the date of nomination to the polling date is quite an expensive proposition. Hon. members on the other side frequently claim that this is true. If we extend that period of time all parties, and even the C.C.F. party, would be faced with an expenditure much greater than the expenditure we are presently obliged to meet in general elections.
